It seems that for pond skating, the appropriate outfit consists of a brown homespun jacket adorned with a fur collar, while those heading to private rinks don a gray herringbone suit paired with a taupe alpine hat. How many barren years I have spent as a skater without such guidance! At last, he broke the silence, asking, “What’s the objective of that game, anyway?” It had never crossed my mind to contemplate that question. Pond skating, particularly under the moonlight, holds a special charm for me. The hollow nestled among the hills always seems to retain a hint of mist, regardless of how clear the sky might be. The shore, which felt like cold iron beneath my feet as I approached the ice, takes on an indistinct quality when viewed from the pond’s center, reminiscent of a dream’s fading memory. Gliding across the surface feels akin to flying within a dream; one floats effortlessly while the world glides beneath. Speed is achieved without strain or intent, as no traces are left behind, and nothing waits to be reached. Like me, the moon serves as the focal point of a circle that is vaguely defined, filled with a continuous stream of impressions that flow through a softly glowing halo of awareness.

I turn to glance at the clock. It reads four-forty. One of the odd side effects of my long tenure as a senior assistant at sea is the tendency to awaken around four in the morning. Her other profession involves selling manuscripts, which creates the bond between us. For the standard agent's commission, she is currently representing one of my works. The newly created chair focusing on the history, literature, and institutions of the United States, which will be shared among various universities in Great Britain, marks a significant departure from the previous exchange professorships that often yielded mixed results. The intent is not to send an American professor annually to Britain to instill them with the “true” culture from its source. Instead, the individual holding this chair will likely be British as often as they are American, and may very well be a public figure rather than an academic. The primary goal is to foster a deeper understanding of the United States in England, and such an aspiration is indeed noble. The ongoing peace and prosperity in the world hinges significantly on how well England comprehends America.

It is a misconception to believe that American understanding of British culture is on par with British understanding of American life. The British Empire represents a substantial and relatively straightforward reality, one that has been in the global spotlight for an extended period. Conversely, the United States, until quite recently, was viewed by the British as a minor entity, albeit a far more intricate one than they assumed. Both sides are acutely aware of each other’s shortcomings, judged through a distinctly familial lens. Americans tend to boast in a nasal tone, while Britons often adopt a condescending manner. Regardless of which nation might emerge victorious in the tumultuous world stage, England ensured its own survival; the American, on the other hand, often settled for the less dignified victories found in commerce, willing to compromise quality of life for financial gain. Nonetheless, Americans have long acknowledged and appreciated the strengths of English political systems, the allure of English living, and the Empire's significant role in fostering freedom and civilization globally. This acknowledgment, however, appears to be reciprocated only by a select few notable British individuals who demonstrate a genuine admiration for America.

In that moment, you find yourself humbled and awed as a resident of the Silent Places.

Even if your only companions are the bats flitting through the darkness and the myriad shadows cast by the trees, those few precious moments spent in the sleeping world provide a profound psychological experience that cannot be replicated. You cannot truly know the night by merely staying awake; she will engage with you when you approach her from the brink of sleep, allowing you to encounter her intimate essence.

Eventually, the night breeze from the river or the wild open spaces begins to chill you. Thoughts of the warmth of your blankets arise, and before long, you find yourself rolling into their soft embrace. And just like that, morning arrives.

Strangely enough, this night of introspection does not leave you to face the day feeling drained. You might feel inclined to retire early, slipping into a slumber with surprising ease, yet your day will commence with clarity and vigor, proceeding energetically and concluding with reserves of energy still intact. You experience no lingering fatigue or dull headaches; instead, those fleeting hours of wakefulness are as restorative as an entire night's sleep.

Mr. Asquith remarked recently, "I have devoted a significant part of my life to advising businessmen on how to extricate themselves from their troubles." This comment was prompted by a group of individuals who were presenting him with the usual complaints about lawyers and the supposed necessity for "businessmen" to take charge of governance. Throughout this war, one of the most tiresome assertions has been the notion of a "business government" and the incessant criticism directed at lawyers.

Personally, I am not a lawyer and do not hold any particular fondness for the profession. I tend to steer clear of their services whenever possible. However, to dismiss lawyers outright as a group is as misguided as claiming that a successful grocer or tailor possesses the qualities of a great statesman simply because of their commercial success. The responsibilities of managing an empire are far more complex than running a grocery store, and it is naive to think that someone who has thrived in the business of selling provisions can automatically govern a nation with insight and wisdom. Take, for example, the most notable grocers of our time—Lord Devonport and Sir Thomas Lipton. Both are undoubtedly commendable individuals, yet would we genuinely consider either of them suitable for the role of Prime Minister? I doubt it.

A great statesman must demonstrate his capabilities through the application of statesmanship, especially under the intense scrutiny of the public eye. While a grocer might make a significant error in his trade without widespread notice, a statesman’s missteps are immediately apparent to all. A statesman must rise to the occasion in the most transparent of conflicts, and those who achieve prominence have invariably proven their mettle through rigorous challenges. This scrutiny does not spare lawyers; Mr. Asquith faced the same trials as Mr. Chamberlain, who was a nail maker, or Mr. Balfour, a landowner. No one derided Mr. Chamberlain as merely a "nailmaker" or Mr. Balfour as simply a "landlord" without adequately addressing their qualifications. So why assume that throwing the term "lawyer" at Mr. Asquith or Mr. Lloyd George suffices to dismiss their abilities?

Nonetheless, the underlying disdain for lawyers does have historical roots. This is not a new phenomenon. Recall Samuel Johnson’s quip when asked about a departed individual: "I dislike making disparaging remarks about someone who isn’t present; however, I believe he is an attorney." Similarly, Carlyle was not much kinder, characterizing barristers as “loaded blunderbusses”—if you paid him, he would obliterate your opponent; if your opponent paid him, he would turn against you. A lawyer’s weapon may be the law, yet their objective is not necessarily justice. Often, the more adept a lawyer is, the more adept they become at circumventing justice. This detachment from the substance of a case and the conscious rejection of moral principles in their professional dealings creates a lingering suspicion around lawyers. They might argue that it is their duty to advocate for their client, while their opponent is tasked with doing the same for theirs, leaving the judge and jury to ensure justice prevails. While that is indeed true, it doesn’t eliminate the skepticism surrounding someone who passionately represents both the guilty and the innocent.

Moreover, lawyers operate in a field that can be quite convoluted. Consider Sancho Panza, who administered justice as Governor of the Island of Barataria; had he been Governor of Britain, he would have enforced the law, and his judgments would have varied significantly. The relationship between law and justice is akin to that between grammar and Shakespeare. If Shakespeare were judged by grammarians, he would likely face condemnation as a rogue and vagabond; similarly, justice frequently suffers at the hands of lawyers. While we recognize the necessity of law, much like grammar, we do not hold an inherent affection for either. They are often perceived as sterile, lifeless disciplines, and those who engage with them can appear suspect. One could be the most unscrupulous individual of their era, yet if one adheres strictly to the law, the lance of justice may never touch them. Law, which ought to serve justice, can often betray its intended purpose.

However, it would be unfair to overlook the progress we have made. Today, the law serves as a more effective instrument of justice than it has in the past, and this improvement is largely attributable to the efforts of distinguished lawyers. While there may be figures reminiscent of Dodson and Fogg in the legal field, there also exist honorable individuals like Pyms and Pratts, who have valiantly defended the liberties of our nation against tyrannical rulers and subservient parliaments.

I find myself standing in the same spot where countless others have stood, gazing up at the magnificent Belfry Tower of Bruges and contemplating, as many have before me, that its design seems to challenge the principles of architectural propriety. Its construction appears intentionally disproportionate, created to elicit a singular, striking impression of height. It resembles a church raised on stilts. This sort of grand yet awkward structure encapsulates the unique spirit and vigor of these Flemish towns. Flanders boasts some of the flattest and most mundane landscapes, yet its buildings are among the most audacious and extravagant. Nature here is subdued; it is civilization that brims with wild energy. The fields stretch out as flat and uniform as a paved plaza, while the streets and rooftops display a chaotic vivacity that resembles a forest whipped by a tempest. The serene waters meander through the countryside as gently as if they flowed through London’s plumbing, yet even the local parish pump is embellished with intricate carvings of wild creatures. This duality reflects a broader truth about art itself. While we often speak of untamed animals, it is humanity that embodies true wildness. In music, there exist sounds that evoke ancient and profound emotions, far surpassing the cries of the most exotic beasts in the dead of night. Similarly, there are structures whose formless strength seems to rise from the earth like primordial monsters, alongside spires that ascend abruptly, reminiscent of startled birds taking flight.

This primal energy manifested in stone speaks to a distinctive aspect of the human spirit. All the creatures of the field maintain a sense of respectability; only humans have truly broken free from decorum. While animals live within the bounds of domestication, it is humanity that often exhibits wild behavior. Furthermore, while this frantic creativity can be found across all human artistic expressions, it is particularly pronounced in Christian art. This notion often leads people to label Christianity as barbaric or a product of ignorance. However, historically speaking, that’s far from the truth; it emerged during one of the most stable and civilized eras in history.

As I continue to gaze at the Belfry, I can’t help but smile at the memory of friends in London who firmly believe that children will inevitably reflect the qualities of what they refer to as “the right environment.” Environment can be a perplexing factor, producing outcomes that are sometimes beneficial, sometimes detrimental, and often a complex blend of both. A beautiful setting might inspire a child to appreciate beauty, or conversely, it could lead to an indifference towards it; most likely, these conflicting influences will cancel each other out. In reality, the impact of one’s environment may be negligible.

In the realm of historical analysis, which once enjoyed popularity and remains conventional today, we often encounter lists attributing the characteristics of nations to their geographic conditions. It has been suggested, for instance, that the Spaniards are passionate due to their warm climate, while Scandinavians are adventurous because of their cold surroundings. Englishmen are said to be seafaring due to their island status, and the Swiss are considered free-spirited thanks to their mountainous terrain. While such observations are appealing, I am equally convinced that I could compile a list that directly counters these claims, demonstrating the opposite influence of geography. For example, Spaniards have charted more continents than their Scandinavian counterparts, despite the former's climate potentially discouraging effort. Likewise, the Dutch have fought valiantly for their freedom, much like the Swiss, even though they lack mountains. Furthermore, many Mediterranean cultures, including Pagan Greece and Rome, have developed a disdain for the sea, despite having the most navigable waters at their disposal. The list could easily go on indefinitely. However, two examples stand out as particularly significant and indisputable. First, the Swiss, who reside beneath awe-inspiring cliffs and glaciers, have produced virtually no art or literature, instead embodying a pragmatic, sensible, and business-oriented ethos. Second, the people of Belgium, who inhabit a landscape as flat as a carpet, have, through an inner drive, aspired to elevate their towers toward the heavens.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the extent to which individuals align with or diverge from their environments, I find little solace in believing that contemporary discussions about environment hold much practical significance. Instead of continuing to dwell on these modern theories, I choose to return my focus to the Belfry of Bruges. I would give these theories more consideration if I were not convinced that they would fade into obscurity long before the Belfry itself ever does.

The challenge presented by cities was one of illumination. How could one guide the residents through the labyrinthine streets once the heavens had withdrawn their celestial lantern? Or, in a more scientific sense, how could they navigate after the Earth had turned away from the sun? The moon, occasionally, provided some assistance; the stars, too, twinkled cheerfully above the rooftops. A beacon here and there on a church or fortress created a picturesque scene and, in the uneven terrain, offered a guiding light for those lost in the darkness. Yet, when the sun, moon, and stars were obscured or absent, the nighttime traveler had to rely on—according to old illustrations—tall, stable lanterns, two stories high. These makeshift lighthouses had numerous holes drilled into their conical roofs, allowing beams of light to shoot forth into the eyes of the bearer. As he ventured into the eerie night, carrying his own source of illumination by a ring on his finger, he experienced the cyclical nature of day and night around him. Shadows loomed over his path, and he felt as if he were being haunted by specters; when the curfew struck, he found himself alone, relying solely on the light he carried in a town enveloped in darkness.

Following the era of portable lanterns in a world of obscurity, a new phase emerged characterized by oil lamps that were notoriously difficult to light and easily extinguished. Their flickering glow was pale and unsteady. The winds of the heavens would blow boisterously, and mischievous children would snuff out the flames, plunging the city back into darkness. Navigating the streets became a challenge, with citizens groping along walls, dining without comfort, and stumbling through muddy gutters. As if the playful winds and rambunctious youths weren’t enough, these fragile lights were often strung between houses, swinging above the thoroughfare. If a gallant general happened to ride by on horseback, passionately pursuing the fate of nations, there was a high likelihood of shattered glass and spilled blood, leaving the street once again in its original state of darkness—untraveled and uncharted, resembling a desolate wasteland.

The conservative, reflecting on the past and the future, finds satisfaction in the progress achieved. His moustache and whiskers had a distinctly military air, yet his posture was uncharacteristically slouched, and his dreamy gaze seemed lost in thought. As our modest pleasure boat approached Yarmouth Harbour, he cast a gloomy yet curious glance at the chaotic array of small vessels that filled the waters. It is well known that entering this harbour is not a straightforward affair; instead of approaching the town directly like a visitor, boats must navigate around the back as if sneaking in like a traitor. The river passage appears almost too constricted for substantial traffic, making the larger ships loom like giants against the sky. As we drifted beneath a timber-laden Norwegian ship that appeared to block the heavens like a grand cathedral, the man in the straw hat pointed at a peculiar wooden figurehead, resembling a woman, and remarked, as if continuing a prior discussion, “Why have they stopped making these? I responded with a lighthearted quip about the captain's wife being envious, yet deep down, I recognized that he had touched upon a profound truth. There is something in our contemporary civilization that seems antagonistic toward such wholesome and beautiful symbols.

“They despise anything that is human and lovely,” he continued, precisely voicing my unspoken thoughts. “I suspect they destroyed all the cheerful old figureheads with hatchets and took pleasure in it.”

“Like Mr. Quilp,” I replied, “when he smashed the wooden Admiral with a poker.”

“Do you come to Yarmouth for that?” he inquired.

“For what?” I asked, puzzled.

“For Dickens,” he clarified, tapping his foot rhythmically on the deck.

“No,” I replied, “I come here for enjoyment, though that isn’t entirely different.”

“I always come,” he stated with a quiet resolution, “to find Peggotty’s boat. It isn’t here.”

At that moment, I fully grasped his sentiment.

Yarmouth exists in two distinct forms; I imagine there are countless renditions in the eyes of its residents. For myself, I have yet to exhaust the list of Batterseas. Yet for visitors and tourists, there are two predominant versions: the impoverished, dignified part and the thriving, garish section. Even the mightiest of heroes must have found their swords sheathed at times during their adventures; in such moments, what would they hold in their right hand? Yet, walking sticks lack any scabbards. My first cane was a malacca, adorned with a silver collar and a polished horn handle. For weeks, it gazed longingly at me from a shop window until a fortunate birthday gift finally allowed me to claim it. Bold black letters proclaimed an intriguing question: “Should Shop Assistants Marry?”

The moment I read those words, it felt as if the world had been turned upside down. The figures of Fleet Street appeared as if they were walking on their hands, and the iconic cross of St. Paul’s seemed suspended in the air in an unnatural position. I realized that I had entered a realm where the belief prevailed that the visible world, represented by the swaying of trees, dictated the existence of the wind. In essence, material conditions, no matter how twisted or bleak, were regarded as more significant than the underlying spiritual truths, regardless of their purity and strength.

Polly is a roan pony, notably plump, and particularly so in recent weeks due to the limited diet of meadow grass. She had been a part of our lives for so long—this is a tale relayed to me by my amiable neighbor during the War, a delightful person known for her patience, especially in croquet—that Polly had become, in the way that ponies often do, a cherished family member. While journalism is meant to strip away the layers of private lives, it often seems to create translucent but blinding barriers between individuals. Whether I find myself in a bustling ballroom or at a packed restaurant, I often pause to consider that among the hundreds of individuals present, there is not a single person whose existence I had previously acknowledged. Yet, each one of them leads a life of tremendous significance—not just to themselves, but also to a multitude of friends and family. Each day, they face their own challenges, and there inevitably comes a moment for each individual when the rest of the world, including—much to my chagrin—myself, seems utterly irrelevant. The fact that I have spent all these years blissfully unaware of their lives fills me with a sense of embarrassment.

Today, dressed in my oldest attire, I have perused the index of The Times Literary Supplement, and I find myself grappling with a profound sense of shame over my lack of knowledge regarding numerous books. The sheer number of novels alone appears to hover around 900. To me, the act of penning even a thoroughly inconsequential novel requires remarkable perseverance; yet, in approximately 600 households, this endeavor has been underway, while I (along with you and countless others) have remained completely apathetic. This morning, I have endeavored to compensate for my previous indifference by examining the titles of these works. While merely reading titles pales in comparison to engaging with the books themselves, it does afford me the luxury of claiming acquaintance with various novels, and in some cases, it even provides a faint hint of their content.

In my estimation, the most enjoyable aspect of crafting a novel must be the selection of a title. A title should encapsulate the essence of the work and offer a prospective reader some insight into what they are about to purchase. Opting for a title like Ethnan Frame, Esther Grant, John Temple, or John Merridew (as noted in the index) fails to assist the reader in any meaningful way. Such titles merely indicate that a character within the pages bears that name, which is likely inconsequential to the reader. Conversely, a title like Phyllis does hint at the nature of the narrative. It suggests that no tragic or intensely realistic story would ever bear the name Phyllis. I would surmise that this novel is a delightful exploration of suburban life, predominantly conveyed through dialogue, featuring Phyllis as an endearing character, albeit somewhat unkind regarding that initial box of chocolates he sent her. Nevertheless, they do end up married in the end.

However, if one chooses not to call their book Phyllis, John Temple, or Mrs. Elmsley, what alternatives exist? You might consider the title Kapak, as I have noticed someone has done. The remarkable aspect of Kapak is that whether you approach the book from the front or the back, it remains unchanged. A title that reads the same in either direction provides substantial advantage to the author. Furthermore, in this instance, there is an element of intrigue surrounding Kapak that compels one to dive deeper. Is it a beloved nickname for a bride’s father-in-law, a secret password to a magical realm, a new product for polishing brown boots, or perhaps merely a camera? One cannot help but feel inclined to purchase the book and uncover the truth.

Another enigmatic title is The Man with Thicker Beard, which likely carries some significance. Like Kapak, it is palindromic, maintaining the same appearance in reverse; however, it lacks the subtlety of its predecessor. Still, it would likely entice readers to explore its contents. On the other hand, A Welsh Nightingale and a Would-be Suffragette is precisely the type of title that would not attract our interest. The mere act of asking a shopkeeper, "Do you have A Welsh Nightingale and a Would-be Suffragette?" feels cumbersome. If we were to forget the title and instead inquire about a would-be nightingale and a Welsh suffragette, or perhaps a wood nightingale and a Welsh rabbit, or even the Welsh suffragette's night in jail, we would rapidly regret not opting for something straightforward like Greed, Earth, or Jonah.

This brings me to the realization that employing a French title often proves to be a misstep. Authors must bear in mind that their readers not only need to order the book verbally but also recommend it to their acquaintances. Thus, I believe Mr. Oliver Onions erred in naming his short story collection Pot au Feu. While it is an appealing title, it poses a challenge for anyone attempting to recommend it, often prompting the response, "What?" When faced with such confusion after attempting to pronounce the title in your best Parisian accent, the only recourse is to shift the topic entirely. Yet, it is high time we reached a consensus on the qualities that constitute an ideal title. Kapak, as mentioned, may attract buyers, though some might find it somewhat unfair. While it excels commercially, it does not fulfill our initial criteria; the title must resonate with the book's essence. In one sense, Five Gallons of Gasolene does achieve this, but admittedly, it is not something one would seek in a bookstore.

Now, consider a title that embodies perfection: Their High Adventure. It conveys just enough meaning on its own. When a Man's Married, For Henri and Navarre, and The King Over the Water are slightly more overt, yet still effective. The Love Story of a Mormon is straightforward, lacking any attempt at deception, but it hardly qualifies as a beautiful title. In contrast, Melody in Silver possesses a certain elegance, yet this very beauty can instill hesitation in a potential buyer, for fear of disappointment lurking within its pages. As I scan the index, I find myself relieved by the multitude of novels I have yet to read. The truth is, many of them would likely lead to disillusionment. Nowadays, one reads books primarily to engage in conversation with others during those rare social outings, asking questions like, "HAVE you read The Forged Coupon, and WHAT are your thoughts on The Muck Rake?" For such exchanges, an index suffices quite well.

The future is uncertain, and while we cannot predict how we will react in dire situations, we are often acutely aware of our limitations. For instance, one might find themselves at a loss in a crisis, such as a fire on a ship or in a building, unsure how to respond amid the chaos. The shock and terror of such emergencies could freeze our instincts or even unleash our primal urges for self-preservation. Although true emotional crises are infrequent, and no amount of preparation can truly equip us for them, we can only hope that we would act appropriately in those moments. Personally, I recognize a fundamental limitation of mine: I am utterly incapable of reciting poetry or performing in front of an audience, regardless of the circumstances. Facing a crowd, even one made up of friends, fills me with a dread that surpasses any physical danger I might encounter. The thought of standing before spectators to express dramatic verses through gestures and expressions sends shivers down my spine.

Watching a skilled reciter perform, no matter how composed they appear, often overwhelms me with embarrassment. Throughout my limited experiences with reciters, I have felt more acutely ashamed for them than they could ever feel for themselves. Even the esteemed actor Brandram, when he adopted a falsetto voice for Shakespeare's female characters, made my face flush with discomfort, compelling me to shut my eyes during his rendition of "Boots at the Holly Tree Inn." However, Brandram was not merely a reciter in the traditional sense; he was more of a solo performer who presented an entire play, sans costumes or sets. The reciters I refer to typically focus on individual pieces and often consist of enthusiastic amateurs who remain undeterred by the scathing critiques in Mr. Anstey's "Burglar Bill," entertaining at various gatherings or smoking concerts. In my youth, the most prominent reciter was the multifaceted Dagonet, who had a notably effective counterpart in the late Mr. Eaton, known for "The Fireman's Wedding." Their era also introduced "Kissing Cup's Race," a piece that Mr. Lewis Sydney and "Q" worked tirelessly to render obsolete. Today, I find myself at a loss regarding the current favorites in recitation, as I have not encountered any in quite some time.

Reflecting on the past, I recall both the best and the worst recitations I have encountered. Among the worst was "Papa's Letter," a poem steeped in cloying sentimentality that could evoke tears from the audience in droves. The story, narrated by a young widow, centers around her golden-haired son who wishes to write to his father. This was prior to Sir Oliver Lodge's advancements in wireless communication between the living and the dead. As the child couldn't write, the mother whimsically transforms him into a letter by placing a stamp on his forehead. He then dashes outside to play but is tragically struck by a runaway horse, and—

The identity of the author of this overly sentimental piece eludes me, although I once spotted W. S. Gilbert's name in a program associated with it. Could it really have been his creation? The psychology behind humor is indeed perplexing.

Turning to the best recitation I remember, I must mention an experience from twenty-five years ago that has only recently been traced back to print. It was performed at a Bohemian gathering I attended in a Fleet Street tavern, where a large Scottish painter, with a visage reminiscent of Falstaff, took the stage. His jovial, ruddy face and exuberantly white hair and beard made quite an impression. I had never crossed paths with him before or after that evening, yet the memory of his presence amidst the swirling tobacco smoke remains vivid. When called upon to share something, the towering figure claimed he would recite James Boswell's authentic opinion of Dr. Johnson. An electric anticipation filled the room, as the artist was renowned for this performance. For someone like me, unfamiliar with the work, the title alone was enticing enough. With a depth of humor that seemed to require crossing borders, he presented the piece while perched tipsily on the edge of an imaginary bed. Each word resonated, and by the conclusion, the grandiose image of the Great Cham was utterly dismantled. For years, I sought this poem, yet no one could provide information about it. Occasionally, I encountered someone who had heard it, but the authorship remained a mystery. It was only last year that I learned the name of the author: Godfrey Turner, a prominent figure in Fleet Street during the 'sixties and 'seventies. A chance meeting with his son led me to various humorous anthologies, one of which, H. S. Leigh's "Jeux d'Esprit," contained the poem. Like many exceptional recitations, it loses its charm when merely read, yet as delivered by the Scottish painter, it came to life in a remarkable way. Here it is; though I suspect there is a mistake at the start of the third stanza unless it reflects Boswell's befuddlement.

In the town of Belfort, I find a seat on the street and observe my surroundings. We often speak in general terms about the archetypal Man in the Street, yet the Frenchman is truly that figure. The elements of daily life that are crucial to him are intertwined with the lamp-posts and sidewalks; every aspect of his existence, from meals to his struggles, is connected to these public spaces. Initially, an English visitor might perceive a French town or village as less visually appealing than those in England. However, with a closer examination, one begins to realize that the lack of picturesque charm largely stems from the stark, flat façades of the houses that rise abruptly from the streets, resembling cardboard sets from a theatrical performance—perhaps a reflection of the rigid nature of French logic. Upon a third glance, it becomes apparent that this is primarily because French homes do not feature front gardens. The English spirit yearns for an entrance that is softened by greenery and interrupted by steps, creating a transitional space that blends indoors and outdoors—a verdant area that serves dual purposes. In contrast, the Frenchman does not require such sentimental barriers, as the street itself feels natural and familiar to him.

While the French may lack front gardens, their streets serve as a collective front garden for everyone. These thoroughfares are adorned with trees and occasionally fountains. The street transforms into the Frenchman’s tavern, where he enjoys a drink; it becomes his dining room, as he often dines outdoors. It also acts as a gallery, as the statues and monuments lining French streets represent the pinnacle of national artistry, often as steeped in history as the Pyramids. Moreover, the street serves as the Frenchman’s Parliament, since the French have historically regarded their Chamber of Deputies with less gravity compared to how the English view their House of Commons. The trivial debates of elected officials confined to formal settings seem trivial to a populace whose ancestors have heard the clarion calls of revolutionaries like Desmoulins or Victor Hugo amidst the backdrop of political upheaval. The street, therefore, is not merely a place for dining and drinking; it is also a battleground where the Frenchman fights and sometimes perishes, imbibing the streets with a significance that transcends the ordinary.

Consider, for instance, the unassuming lamp-post. In London, a lamp-post can evoke humor, as one might picture a drunken man leaning against it, reminiscing about old friendships. However, in Paris, it carries a weight of tragedy, conjuring images of tyrants being hanged and the world coming to an end. There was a satirical Republican newspaper in Paris called LA LANTERNE, and one might find amusement at the thought of a British publication titled THE LAMP POST. We have established that the Frenchman embodies the essence of the man in the street, dining and dying in that very locale. If I were to wander through Paris and witness him settling down for the night in the street, it would only reaffirm his alignment with the spirit of his culture. All that is virtuous and all that is vice in France is intertwined with this outdoor ethos. French democracy, alongside its indecencies, reflects a desire for life to unfold in the open air. In comparison, a café possesses a more public character than a British public house.

Two particular reasons prompted these reflections while I wandered the streets of Belfort. For one, this town is located near the border of France and Germany, and boundaries are among the most beautiful concepts in existence. To truly love something often means to embrace its edges. Children instinctively gravitate toward the perimeters of things, building sandcastles along the shore or playing on the fringes of grass, only restrained by rules and authority. Reaching the conclusion of one experience often signifies the dawn of another.

Consequently, Belfort appears even more quintessentially French precisely because it lies on the very edge of Germany. Despite the German influences present in the area—such as German names, larger beer mugs, and theatrical barmaids dressed in exaggerated Alsatian costumes—the dominant French character seems to be intensified by these foreign elements. All day and night, groups of weary, sun-kissed soldiers trudge through the streets, emanating an air of stubborn disdain. German soldiers may exude contempt, but French soldiers possess a dual disdain, directed both at themselves and at others. This realism, perhaps, is an integral part of a nation skilled in war, science, and other undertakings that necessitate a blend of the essential and the unpleasant. Both soldiers and civilians often sport cropped hair and possess a certain robust appearance, which to an English observer might seem nearly brutal, a quality we might call “bullet-headed.” Indeed, it is fitting that we label it thus, for the intellectual evolution of the French has often mirrored the trajectory of bullets—yes, even those that explode.

Yet another reason to contemplate the open-air politics and art of the French in this town lies in its reputation for housing one of the most iconic public monuments in the nation. From my café seat, I can gaze upon the hill that looms over the town, crowned by a substantial, flat-faced citadel, its many windows glowing in the evening sun. At the base of this steep hill rests a colossal stone lion, as imposing as the hill itself. The monument has been carved from the rock in a manner that eschews triviality; it is not designed to resemble a typical statue, nor does it seek to render the lion’s mane in delicate curls or delineate the creature sharply from the earth from which it emerges, as if shaking the world itself. The lion's visage possesses a bold conventionality reminiscent of Assyrian artistry, and its mane is rendered as a shapeless tempest cloud, as if to suggest that divine forces have adorned its neck with thunder. Even from afar, the structure appears monumental, almost prehistoric, despite its relatively recent origin. It commemorates the town's unwavering resistance against the Germans throughout a harrowing year, surrendering only at the behest of its own government. Yet, the essence of defiance and resilience has pervaded this land since time immemorial.

As I depart this town and board a train into Germany, the news becomes increasingly urgent, filtering through the streets that Southern France is ablaze, hinting at the potential culmination of a grim modern struggle between wealth and poverty. As I traverse into more tranquil regions, I catch one last glimpse of the Lion of Belfort, standing proudly against the skyline—the final sight of a great nation that has known little peace.

The rain fell steadily as Victor Crummles stepped out onto the pavement. However, the weather was the least of his concerns. He raised his umbrella instinctively, not truly registering the action. His thoughts were consumed by the daunting task ahead. “I’m really in a bind,” he reminded himself, glancing at the piece of paper in his pocket that indicated where and when he was due for a medical examination. Reassuring himself, he confirmed its presence: Kilburn. Twelve o’clock.

Indeed, he found himself in quite a predicament. But he quickly reassured himself that he didn’t mind it at all. His patriotism ran deep, and he felt a strong desire to contribute to the war effort. He longed to take on the Germans and show them what he was made of. If only he had been younger, he thought; he would have enlisted without hesitation. But at thirty-eight, he felt the weight of his age.

As he approached the “Golden Crown,” he considered stopping for “just one.” A drink would bolster his spirits and prepare him for the doctors. After all, he believed he ought to give them a fair chance, regardless of the potential ramifications for himself. A whisky-and-soda would surely help him feel "in the pink."

With the drink consumed, he felt a surge of confidence. It was time to make his way to Kilburn. He contemplated his travel options. It was at least a two-mile journey—plenty of distance to cover. He could catch the bus, or take the Tube, but walking seemed the best choice in the end. There was time to spare. Besides, he needed to consider his varicose vein. The doctors should be informed; it wouldn’t be right to conceal such information from them. Varicose veins were serious conditions, and he had done his research. He could recall the definition clearly:

“The dilation and thickening of veins, accompanied by lengthening and tortuosity, leading to the formation of knots or knobs, where blood coagulates, fibrin deposits, and sometimes even bone matter develops; additionally, the vein walls are diseased.”

This was no trivial matter. Many men had been disqualified due to similar issues, and it was only fair the doctors were made aware of his condition. Regardless, it was imperative that the doctors see his leg in its true condition.

He believed it was wrong to let patriotism cloud his honesty. He felt a moral duty to avoid deceiving his country, especially considering the financial resources that would be wasted on someone who might falter early in service. He wanted to fight for his nation as much as anyone else, but he also understood the responsibility he bore. It was essential to prioritize the country’s interests over his own desires.

Yes, he decided, it was his obligation to walk. It was crucial that he disclose the details of his varicose vein. He hoped it wouldn’t be a disqualifying factor, but he was committed to being forthright no matter the outcome. He wouldn’t misrepresent himself; he would ensure that the doctor fully understood the state of his leg.

When Victor finally entered the examination room, fatigue washed over him, but he steeled himself. He had indulged in another drink at the “Spread Eagle” and felt ready to face whatever awaited him. The room was occupied by two doctors—one seated at a desk, the other standing near a window.

“Anything bothering you?” the seated doctor inquired.

“Not that I’m aware of,” Victor replied, adopting a serious demeanor. However, he begrudgingly added, “I do have a bit of a varicose vein, but it’s hardly worth mentioning.”

“Oh, don’t worry about that,” the doctor assured him. “We’ve moved past that point. Now, strip.”

“Don’t worry about that? Moved past that point?” Victor pondered the implications. He had done his duty by mentioning the condition. If there was indeed fibrin or osseous matter in his veins, he had provided ample warning. It was the nation that would bear the consequences. Doctors could be so dismissive sometimes.

“Stripped? Alright, let’s take a look at you,” the doctor commanded.

The examination commenced, and Victor wondered if his varicose vein might actually astonish the doctor. He had walked two miles, and it should be noticeable—though he didn’t necessarily wish for it to be. If his condition was significant, it was only fair that the doctors were informed.

“What did you say your age was?” the doctor asked.

“Thirty-eight, sir,” Victor replied.

“Thirty-eight! Thirty-eight… um… Jeffkins!” the doctor called to his colleague, who joined him in assessing Victor. They appeared to disregard his leg entirely. If they overlooked it, he wouldn’t be responsible if something went awry.

“You can get dressed,” the first doctor announced before stepping aside with Jeffkins to whisper to each other.

After a moment, the first doctor returned. “Well, my man, it won’t do,” he declared. “We admire your spirit… very commendable, indeed. But (laughing) thirty-eight? Come now.”

A realization struck Victor. Was he truly being rejected? And for being too old? The thought filled him with shame and frustration, especially since he was eager to fight the enemy.

“But upon my word…” he began earnestly.

“There, there, we understand,” the doctor replied. “You’ve done your best, and it’s commendable. But thirty-eight! Really now… Good morning.”

Once outside, Victor was engulfed by a tumult of emotions that he could not endure alone. He turned back toward the “Spread Eagle,” seeking solace in the familiar surroundings as he grappled with the bitter disappointment of his rejection.

A few weeks ago, I relocated to a new home, and naturally, my books made the journey alongside me. Strong men, sweaty from exertion, packed them into boxes and lugged them to the moving van, grumbling about Caxton as they worked. Upon reaching my new place, they carried the boxes into the designated room for my library, removed the lids, and awaited further instructions. My immediate concern was to clear out the empty room. In a hurry, we moved the books onto the pristine white shelves that had been prepared for them, prioritizing getting them off the floor over any particular order. We stacked armful after armful hastily, with only a brief pause when the foreman’s eye caught one of my titles. "Did you write this one, sir?" he inquired. I admitted it, and he replied with a noncommittal "H'm," before looking through the remaining stacks and appearing slightly taken aback by the number of titles I had not authored. It seems writing is a rather relaxed profession.

Eventually, the books found their place on the shelves, and there they remain. I told myself that I would organize them properly when a rainy day presented itself. When that rainy day finally arrived, I instead pushed the task to some future morning. As things stand, finding a specific book requires scanning every shelf, and encountering Keats offers no assurance of being close to Shelley. If he hasn’t mysteriously vanished, he’s likely wedged between How to Be a Golfer Though Middle-aged and something else equally perplexing.

Having penned that observation, I felt compelled to check where Shelley actually resided on my shelves. The situation is worse than I had anticipated. He is currently lodged between Geometrical Optics and Studies in New Zealand Scenery. Ella Wheeler Wilcox, whom I had unwittingly invited into my collection, shares a space with Anarchy or Order, a title that was apparently sent in hopes of persuading me to join the Duty and Discipline Movement—a hope that seems futile, as I have yet to fulfill my subscription. Meanwhile, What I Found Out, an account by an English Governess, occupies a corner with The Recreations of a Country Parson, followed closely by Villette and Baedeker's Switzerland. Clearly, I need to take action. Yet, I find myself pondering what that action should be. If I misled you into believing my books were neatly organized in their previous shelves, I apologize. They were arranged in what one might call "all anyhow." Perhaps they were slightly less "anyhow" than they are now, as volumes of the same work were at least grouped together, but that’s about the extent of their order. For years, I avoided the task of tidying them up, just as I’m continuing to do now. It isn’t due to laziness; rather, I am simply at a loss regarding where to start.

Let’s consider the idea of grouping all the poetry together. This seems reasonable at first glance. However, there’s an issue of size: Byron stands a towering eleven inches tall (he is my tallest poet), while Beattie, my shortest, is just over four inches. Placing them side by side would result in a rather absurd sight. You may not be familiar with Beattie, but rest assured, he was indeed a poet. He composed those grand lines about the shepherd:

"The shepherd-swain of whom I mention made  
On Scotia's mountains fed his little flock;  
The sickle, scythe or plough he never swayed—  
An honest heart was almost all his stock."

It’s hardly reasonable to expect a shepherd to wield a plow in the conventional manner, but Beattie appropriately highlighted that Edwin, the shepherd-swain, didn’t either. "And yet poor Edwin was no vulgar boy," we learn later in a line that deserves to endure. Now that I’ve established Beattie’s legitimacy as a poet, I can return to my point: an eleven-inch Byron cannot be positioned alongside a four-inch Beattie and followed by an eight-inch Cowper without creating an awkward shelf display. Yet, how could I possibly discard Beattie—Beattie, who wrote:

"And now the downy cheek and deepened voice  
Gave dignity to Edwin's blooming prime."

For those of us from England, the magnitude of such financial offers is quite foreign compared to the American landscape. I wrapped a damp cloth around my head and attempted to analyze the staggering figures with a detached perspective, though it was challenging to do so when they resembled fortunes fit for kings. Additionally, he was offered a signing bonus of one hundred thousand dollars and fifty percent of any profits generated from his films after the payment of his salary. Yet, he declined the entire offer.

This situation is truly remarkable, illustrating that the public's craving for humor can lead a diminutive, eccentric man—characterized by his splay feet and peculiar antics with a cigarette, a hat, and a cane—to be offered and subsequently reject such immense wealth, all for the simple act of entertaining through the medium of film. The peculiarity of this scenario is heightened when one considers that these astounding figures emerged during wartime. Chaplin's ascent to wealth and influence coincided with one of history's most brutal conflicts.

If there is a fundamental need for humor, then Charlie’s career is undoubtedly validated. He stands as the first comedian to achieve global acclaim. I often wonder if the man known as the Funniest Man on Earth fully comprehends his significance. Does he gaze into the mirror and reflect on the familiarity of his face, which has become more recognizable than any other?

Now, standing at fifty years of age, I do not feel like an artifact at all; instead, I feel as youthful as I ever did. I had feared that entering middle age would bring with it a sense of nostalgia for the joys of my youth, a longing for the past that would make life feel unbearable. I worried about how life would be once cricket—a cherished pastime—lost its importance in my daily routine. The thought of never again experiencing the thrill of a perfect shot to the boundary or the satisfaction of catching an opponent in the slips painted a bleak picture of the future. Yet, I’ve come to realize that the essence of youth is not contingent upon cricket or childhood delights. It is rooted in an acceptance of the possibilities life offers. So, do not assume, my younger friend, that your ability to leap five feet eight inches makes you younger than I am just because I have no desire to jump anymore. The spirit of youth is a far deeper and more persistent quality than mere physical prowess. It can flourish just as vibrantly at eighty as it does at eighteen; only its expressions may shift over time. Holmes famously declared that he never felt old, proclaiming, “I am eighty-three young today.” Likewise, Johnson, despite his age and ailments, insisted he was “a young fellow”—and indeed, he embodied a sprightly spirit that defied the ravages of time.

Youth is, in truth, not merely a physical condition but rather a matter of the soul. One can feel spiritually aged at twenty-five or retain a lively, youthful spirit at eighty. Byron lamented his own decline at the tender age of thirty-four, expressing sentiments of lifelessness and decay. While there may have been an element of self-dramatization in his words, the fact remains that he had aged into an old man by thirty-six, whereas Browning, who lived to seventy-seven, maintained an unyielding spirit of youth to the very end, encapsulated in the vibrant finale of “Asolando.”

When contemplating old age, it is a common misstep to assume that the spirit must diminish alongside the body. Naturally, if the body is treated poorly, its consequences will affect the spirit. However, the natural decline of our physical capabilities does not have to weaken the healthy spirit; in fact, it can fortify it. This spirit, while perhaps lacking the fervor of youth, can burn more steadily with the passage of time. In our younger days, our restless spirits often long for unattainable dreams.

The scope of our aspirations may narrow, but the vastness of our existence remains unchanged, leading to the realization that what truly matters is often right at our fingertips. During a conversation steeped in nostalgia, the Bishop sought to draw out the Archdeacon’s memories of yesteryear. Suddenly, the Archdeacon shifted the topic, asking, “What was the Philharmonic concert like last night?” When the Bishop expressed surprise, the Archdeacon explained, “Though I am an elderly man, I strive to keep my heart young, and the best way to achieve that is to ensure my thoughts remain aligned with the vibrant life around me rather than dwelling on the past.”

The reality is that each phase of our journey holds its unique attractions. None is necessarily superior to another, though I have always favored the stage in which I currently find myself. At twenty, I believed there was no age quite like that, and now that I am fifty, I have transferred my enthusiasm to this present age. I genuinely believe that if fortune permits me to reach sixty, I will proclaim that there is no age like sixty. And why not? The beauty of witnessing the sun rise over morning hills is matched by the pleasure of strolling homeward as evening shadows stretch and the coolness of twilight sets in.

When the eighteen-handicap golfer peruses the impressive achievements of renowned players, he feels no jealousy. Over time, he has unraveled the profound allure of golf. Initially, he pondered what made it so captivating; now, he understands that golf enjoys its popularity because it is the ideal game for those who struggle with it.

Take, for instance, the experience of being poor at cricket. You've invested in a new bat, perfectly balanced; a pristine pair of pads; and gloves featuring the latest innovations. Are you allowed to showcase them? Certainly not. After just one delivery, during which your bat, pads, and gloves remain untouched, you’re sent back to the pavilion to endure an afternoon filled with tedious tales from an elderly gentleman who once knew Fuller Pilch. When your team fields, where are you positioned? Likely at long leg, exposed to the audience as possibly the worst fielder in the city. The emotional toll is crushing—regret, frustration, humiliation, and above all, envy of those fortunate souls who play effortlessly on the hallowed grounds of Lord's.

Now, think about being inept at lawn tennis. While you are permitted to hold onto your new racket throughout the match, how frequently do you get to use it effectively? Your partner often shouts “Mine!” and shoves you aside. Is there any joy in playing football poorly? You might wear your new boots for the entire match, yet your interactions with the ball remain minimal. In football, the ball doesn’t belong to you.

In stark contrast, golf welcomes the less skilled player. In golf, the less proficient individual receives the most strokes. Regardless of the opponent’s skill level, the novice golfer has the right to complete each hole, thus enjoying more of the game. There’s no need to worry that their new driver will sit idle; they are guaranteed ample opportunity to swing it, perhaps even more than the proficient player if they miss the ball entirely on a tee. A new niblick promises immediate enjoyment right from the first round.

Observing these immense beings writhing under the influence of an invisible and violent energy brings to mind a memory of a young boy I once knew. During a stroll through Battersea Park on a day much like this, with dark skies and swaying trees, he exhibited a profound dislike for the wind. It blasted into his face, forced his eyes shut, and swept off his favorite hat, which he wore with great pride. If memory serves me right, he was around four years old at the time. After many complaints about the chaotic weather, he finally turned to his mother and exclaimed, “Well, why don’t you take away the trees, and then it wouldn’t wind.”

It is entirely natural and understandable to assume that the trees are responsible for creating the wind. This belief is so common and justifiable that it mirrors the views of nearly all contemporary philosophers, reformers, sociologists, and politicians in our era. My young friend, in this regard, was much like many leading thinkers today, though undeniably more charming.

In the little parable he inadvertently crafted, the trees symbolize all tangible entities, while the wind represents the intangible. The wind embodies the spirit that moves freely as it wishes; the trees signify the material world that is swayed by this spirit's whims. We recognize the existence of the wind when we observe the trees on a distant hill suddenly thrashing about. Similarly, we acknowledge a genuine revolution only when we see the rooftops of a city trembling in a frenzy.

A distinguished naval officer once posed a question to me regarding the origins of Davy Jones, leaving me speechless and embarrassed. The embarrassment should have belonged to him, given his position within the Admiralty, where knowledge of maritime lore is expected. However, the whims of circumstance found me, a mere literary figure, feeling the weight of that moment.

With my head bowed, I resolved that upon my return to London and access to books, I would uncover the truth. But have I truly discovered it? That is for you to determine.

I commenced my inquiry with a "Glossary of Sea Terms," which offered a slick explanation regarding Davy Jones's locker but failed to address its etymology. I then progressed to "The Oxford Dictionary," where the definition was presented with greater clarity, including guidance on the pronunciation of Davy’s name. Many might presume that it is pronounced as it appears—simply Davy—but the late Dr. Murray had a different perspective. The correct pronunciation is Dē.vi. After navigating this confusion, the Dictionary elaborated on nautical slang, defining Davy Jones as “the spirit of the sea, the sailor's devil,” and described Davy Jones’s locker as the ocean, particularly as a grave for those who meet their demise at sea. Among the references was Smollett’s "Peregrine Pickle," along with one J. Willock, whom I will revisit later.

Determined to trace the origin of Davy Jones, I turned to "The Dictionary of National Biography," which, despite its limitations in being unavailable for casual reading ashore, remains an invaluable resource—arguably more essential than the Bible or works by Boswell, Plato, and others, should one find themselves stranded on a desert island. To my surprise, I discovered eight individuals named David Jones, all of Welsh descent; yet none could be directly linked to the legendary figure in question. Among them were hymn-writers, a revivalist, a soldier and translator, a barrister, a missionary to Madagascar (the only one with any maritime experience), and a fervent preacher whose life challenges turned his hair from coal-black to white overnight—an eventuality mine seemed destined to follow.

Reflecting on my approach, it occurred to me that I should have consulted "Notes and Queries" first, where I was promptly rewarded. This publication had addressed the very question back in 1851. On June 14, that year, a Mr. Henry Campkin sought assistance from the periodical, which, given its nautical motto courtesy of Captain Cuttle, should have welcomed inquiries of this nature. Unlike my Admiralty acquaintance, Mr. Campkin did not bluntly inquire, "Who the devil was Davy Jones?" Instead, he posed the question in a gentlemanly fashion, asking, "Who was the significant individual whose name has become such a powerful myth? And what led to the ocean being identified with the locker of this enigmatic figure?"

Mr. Campkin's request was answered remarkably quickly—much faster than one might expect today. By June 21, Mr. Pemberton, the only reader of "Notes and Queries" to rise to the occasion, provided an answer that would serve as a cornerstone for our understanding. As a seafarer himself, Mr. Pemberton had pondered the question at length and proposed that the name Davy Jones might have originated from the biblical prophet Jonah (who, notably, was not Welsh but an Israelite). While Jonah was not precisely a sailor, his own seafaring exploits are well-documented; in his prayer, he reflects upon his experiences with the ocean: "The waters compassed me about... the depth closed me round about; the weeds were wrapped about my head," and so forth. Thus, Pemberton posited, the sea might be fittingly referred to as Jonah's locker by an unrefined mariner, and the name Jonah could naturally have morphed into Jones. Given that many Welshmen (including Mr. Lloyd George, from whom we derive stirring oratory) are often named Davy, it follows that "Davy Jones" would eventually emerge. This theory from Mr. Pemberton appears to be the sole explanation I have encountered, though I suspect Mrs. Gamp might lend her support—albeit with a humorous twist, preferring a different term for "locker" that comic military poets often rhyme with "réveillé."

On the first day of May, I found myself seated outside a café in Place de la Bastille in Paris, gazing at the triumphant column topped with a lively figure. This monument commemorates the spot where the populace dismantled a prison and ushered in a new era. It serves as a fascinating illustration of how much of human history is steeped in symbolism. In terms of physical reality, the Bastille was hardly a dreadful prison when it fell; it was barely a prison at all. Yet, it became an emblem, and people possess an innate knack for recognizing symbols. For example, during the last General Election, the figure of the Chinaman or President Kruger’s hat in the preceding election showcased this instinct.

The Chinaman, with his distinctive pigtail, embodies precisely what the people resented about African policy—the foreign and bizarre nature of wealth, the unsettling truth that money lacks roots, that it operates not as a natural force but rather as an insidious magic that summons monsters from distant lands. The populace harbored a deep-seated aversion towards the mine owner who could effortlessly transport a Chinaman across oceans, much like they detested the sorcerer who could conjure a flying dragon. Similarly, Mr. Kruger’s hat was not merely a joke; it symbolized precisely what stirred impatience and anger among the people—a drab, archaic, Republican simplicity, the unappealing dignity of the bourgeoisie, and the weighty platitudes of political morality. While people may sometimes err in practical political matters, they are seldom mistaken when it comes to the artistic realm.

This phenomenon undoubtedly applied to the Bastille as well. The act of demolishing the Bastille transcended mere reform; it represented a more profound iconoclasm, the shattering of a stone idol. To the people, the structure loomed like a giant with countless eyes, and they struck at it as if it were a carved reality. "Have you heard the latest?"

It was the landlord of the Blue Boar who interrupted me as I walked down the village lane, a meandering path lined with a handful of thatched cottages and several barns. His face radiated excitement, and it was clear he had some significant news to share. As a former soldier, his opinions on the war carry considerable weight in our community. I hadn’t yet caught wind of the news, but the landlord’s broad grin assured me it was something positive.

“Jim has received a commission,” he announced, his tone unmistakably conveying that this development would set events in motion. Jim is his son, a sergeant-major in the artillery, who has been stationed at the front since the early days of the conflict.

The announcement sent ripples of excitement through the village. However, we’ve become somewhat desensitized to such news, as this year has delivered an avalanche of remarkable occurrences. Just recently, thousands of soldiers from a large encampment located ten miles away descended upon our area, engaging in an intense two-day battle in the surrounding hills. They trampled through hedgerows, camped in the cornfields, damaged the apple trees in my orchard, and even commandeered tea from the local residents, transforming our quiet village into a scene of chaotic thrill.

“I’ve never seen anything like it in my life,” old Benjamin remarked to me later that evening. “I’ve lived in that bungalow for eighty-five years come Michaelmas, and I’ve never witnessed anything like this before. Yes, eighty-five years come Michaelmas. My father had that land on a peppercorn rent, and the way he lost it was like this—”

Just as Benjamin began his familiar tale of grievance, a sudden commotion among the soldiers provided me with an escape from his recounting.

Who could have imagined that we would someday hear French spoken casually in our village? Yet here we are. At the far end of the lane, a family of Belgians has settled into a small cottage, remnants of the tide of refugees that followed the turmoil of 1914. Their experiences have brought the harsh realities of war uncomfortably close, having fled the horrors of Louvain, where they hid in cellars for days while two of their children lost their lives, ultimately escaping to the coast on foot.

Armed with this guide, there would be little excuse for failing to learn the names of the bride and groom at a wedding. Additionally, it offers a list of synonyms for common subjects of description, which I find to be quite generous. John Stuart Mill's concern that the sounds of the piano might eventually fade away is trivial compared to my anxiety that a day will arrive when whimsical literature will vanish from the quaint old bookshops, leaving no treasures for my eyes to discover. In an effort to restore my faith in the existence of such literary gems, a friend has sent me a copy of "The Compleat English Physician, or The Druggist's Shop Opened (the like not hitherto extant)" by William Salmon, who dated his preface "From my house at the Blew Ball by the Ditch-side near Holborn Bridge, London, May 5, 1693." This comprehensive volume draws from all realms of creation—animal, vegetable, and mineral—to offer remedies for human afflictions, and in the dedication, the author extends his services to the Most Serene and Illustrious Princess Mary II., should she require his medicinal expertise.

The "Dictionary of National Biography," which omits mention of this particular work, notes that William Salmon was born in 1644 and received his education under a mountebank. After a period of travel, he established himself in London as an unconventional practitioner, dealing in pills for every ailment, complete with horoscopes. There was speculation during his lifetime that he may not have been the original source of the extensive knowledge reflected in his numerous volumes, but rather an amanuensis. The "Dictionary" corroborates this theory; however, in the preface to "The Compleat English Physician," Salmon vehemently defends himself against one critic, whom he describes as "the nasty author of an impertinent and scurrilous pamphlet," asserting that he has accumulated thirty years of practical pharmacy experience. Yet, it seems improbable that even three decades of diligent work could suffice to gather the vast array of insights found within this remarkable tome.

It is both an ironic and frustrating reality that we possess within ourselves the cures for all the afflictions our bodies endure.

In most scientific fields, contemporary scholars possess more knowledge than those who came before them. Knowledge tends to build upon itself over time. However, after perusing Salmon's twelve hundred pages, one cannot help but feel relieved that the practice of medicine has become significantly more straightforward since 1693. The next time we call upon a physician, we should express gratitude for their modern incompleteness. In Salmon's era, a doctor, brimming with confidence in their comprehensive understanding, might have prescribed a treatment derived from our recently deceased neighbor.

After detailing the restorative properties of the human body, Salmon shifts his focus to Alces, the Elk; Antilopus, the Antelope; and Asinus, the Ass. Every creature serves a therapeutic purpose for humanity, but few are as valuable as the Ass. While a living donkey has its merits, it pales in comparison to the extensive benefits derived from a deceased donkey transformed into medicinal compounds. Equus, the Horse; Capra, the Goat; and Cercopithecus, the Monkey, each serve as well-stocked apothecaries in their own right. Indeed, anything that moves, whether on two legs or four, yields potent elixirs, yet it is the inclusion of humanity in this mix that is jarring. It seems appropriate for the Lord of Creation to extract remedies from his soulless inferiors, but to do so from himself is a disheartening notion.

The avian world also contributes to this pharmacopoeia. For example, the flesh of Alauda, the Lark, can alleviate colicky pains—a thought to keep in mind when visiting Ye Old Cheshire Cheese. Alcedo, the Kingfisher, when reduced to powder and combined with ground human skull and a hint of amber salt, proves effective against epilepsy. A number of swallows, when pulverized in a mortar (a grim thought indeed!), yield a substance that can prevent seizures. The flesh of Lucinia, the Nightingale, is said to help those suffering from consumption, while its gall mixed with honey creates an excellent eye wash. The true danger to our society lies in the potential for its mechanisms to become overly rigid, even as its spirit becomes increasingly capricious. A man’s minor choices and routines should remain adaptable, fluid, and imaginative; what should remain steadfast are his principles and ideals. Yet, in our current reality, the opposite holds true; our opinions shift frequently, while our lunch remains unchanged. I would prefer for individuals to hold strong, enduring beliefs, but as for their meals, they ought to enjoy them in the garden, in bed, on the roof, or even perched high in a tree. Let them debate from the same foundational ideas, but do so in a bed, a boat, or a balloon. This troubling rise of rigid habits reflects an excessive focus on virtues that mere convention can assure, while neglecting those deeper values that cannot be guaranteed by routine—values of spontaneous compassion or candid honesty. A man can become accustomed to rising at five in the morning, but adapting to being persecuted for one’s beliefs is often a fatal first trial. We ought to pay closer attention to the potential for the heroic and the unexpected. I suspect that upon leaving my bed, I may embark on some act of remarkable virtue.

The cheerful disposition of the blind continually fascinates me. It seems that when the external light fades, an inner brilliance ignites, illuminating the shadows that surround them. Outside, the night may be dark and foreboding, yet within, there exists a warmth and radiance. The world becomes confined to the realm of one’s thoughts, yet this very limitation appears to elevate the spirit, causing it to soar with greater fervor. He remarked, “How quickly the sun has set,” only to be told by a companion that it had not yet set. In that instant, he became completely blind. Yet those who knew him claimed that his mental vivacity never diminished during his years of blindness; in fact, it flourished.

Aldenham's pond, situated a short stroll from the house, is easily accessible via a well-maintained gravel path, allowing visitors to reach its edge without getting muddy, regardless of the weather. This makes it possible to gauge the previous night's rainfall by observing the water level. Some irreverently refer to it as the "hippopotamus pond," likening it to the habitat of a hippopotamus at the zoo, where the creature often remains submerged, hidden from view. Yet, for most of us, it is simply known as "the pond," a name that conveniently overlooks the presence of other nearby natural ponds and attributes its existence solely to human endeavor. In truth, it is a modest, man-made structure crafted from cement, lacking any ostentation.

The pond features seven steps, each measuring 10 inches in height, which unintentionally transform it into an effective rain gauge. When the water covers three steps, as it did last Monday, it indicates that approximately 40 inches of rain have accumulated since the pond began filling last month. This fact may astonish newcomers, but it is crucial to reveal the underlying secret: much of the surrounding land drains into the pond as well. This offers a more accurate reflection of rainfall than the official measurements reported in the newspapers. After a day of disrupted cricket due to rain, it feels absurd to be told that only .026 of an inch caused the chaos; one yearns for a more dramatic figure. The pond's record of an additional 5 inches of rain brings a sense of comfort, whereas the dry statistics from a conventional rain gauge would likely frustrate us. It speaks volumes about Aldenham's insightful perspective that he designed the pond with this understanding in mind.

After years of battling against oppression, I find myself tethered to a different kind of bondage: I now possess a telephone.

While there are numerous benefits to having this device, it has also deprived me of one of life's rarest and most delightful experiences—the thrill of making a three-pence call from a public call box without having to pay. Over the years, this extraordinary occurrence has happened to me only twice. Just last week, I encountered a wealthy man, typically somber in demeanor, whose face lit up with a triumphant grin as he recounted that it had also occurred to him recently.

On the flip side, owning a telephone offers me the opportunity to avoid one of life's most common and tiresome frustrations: the excruciating wait outside a call office while the person inside engages in a conversation that is not only trivial but seems to stretch on indefinitely. In London, these call offices serve both men and women; however, in the suburbs, they are predominantly frequented by women, who may appear to be romantically involved but are often just reminding their husbands to pick up the fish. Nonetheless, having my own telephone does not completely eliminate the agony of waiting. If a fairy godmother were to appear before me—though, after all these years, I am not particularly optimistic about such an occurrence—and grant me a wish, I would deliberate long before settling on anything more significant than reclaiming all the time I’ve wasted with the telephone pressed to my ear, awaiting a response. The usual waits can feel lengthy, but nothing quite compares to the sensation of eternity when one sits at the device while someone is fetched from another part of the building. This experience is not just a glimpse of eternity; it feels like a descent into despair, for there is nothing to occupy the mind. When left to idle, time drags on interminably. Even if a book happens to be at hand, reading is impossible as one’s thoughts cannot wander freely; all that occupies the mind is the anxious speculation about the messenger's progress, the current activity of the person being sought, and the potential journey they are undertaking to reach the receiver. In this preoccupation, minutes, hours, days, and even weeks appear to stretch out in reluctant agony.

Lastly, I propose that, while it is beyond the reach of legal enforcement, it should become customary for editors to ensure the publication of letters containing clear and actionable complaints. There has been an alarming trend of editors becoming far too lax in this regard. In earlier times, an editor took on the role of an unofficial public servant, charged with the responsibility of conveying public discourse. If an editor chose to suppress content, it was expected that they would have a compelling reason, such as the material being defamatory or indecent. In contrast, today's editors often view themselves as creative artists who can curate and censor information with the same casualness as a poet or caricaturist. They may include a particular letter simply because they deem it clever, while dismissing others they consider trivial. The suppression of an article may occur if they perceive it as incorrect, while a more concerning piece might be withheld because they deem it appropriate. The traditional view that the editor is merely a conduit for public expression—a true "organ" of opinion—seems to have been entirely lost. In contemporary times, the editor is not just the medium; they are also the performer manipulating that medium.

This shift encapsulates the pressing danger of our era. The oppression witnessed in the past often involved individual actors—both the oppressors and the oppressed were straightforward and isolated in their struggles. The aristocrat may have harbored disdain for those beneath them, yet they also resented their peers. The capitalist often operated as an individualist. However, in our current age, even capitalists have adopted a façade of Socialism. They now possess the advantage of scientific advancement and collective organization, enabling them to potentially establish a tyranny far greater than anything previously experienced.

It has been quite some time since I experienced the thrill of falling in love, and as I gaze into the mirror, noting what Holmes refers to as "Time's visiting cards" adorning my face and hair, I come to the realization that I may never again partake in such an experience. To echo Mr. Kipling's soldier:

That's all shuv be'ind me Long ago and fur away.

Yet, as Wordsworth suggested, poetry is emotion recollected in tranquility, and it is only when you have moved past the experience of love that you can genuinely articulate it or discuss it with the necessary philosophical objectivity.

Falling in love is, of course, not the challenging part; anyone can do that. The real challenge lies in discerning whether the feelings you are experiencing are authentic or merely a facade. Many individuals misinterpret their emotions and only realize, when it is far too late, that they have never truly experienced genuine love. This misunderstanding contributes to the backlog in Divorce Courts. It also highlights the significance of "calf love," which serves as a formative experience, helping one to differentiate between the essence of love and its mere semblance.

When I refer to "calf love," I am not including the vague inklings of early childhood, reminiscent of those immortalized in "Annabel Lee":

I was a child and she was a child In that kingdom by the sea.

* * * * *

Yet we loved with a love that was more than love, I and my Annabel Lee.

I recall that love vividly; it blossomed when I was merely eight years old. "She" was also eight, having just returned from India. Admittedly, she was not conventionally attractive, but—well, she had come from India. The very essence of that distant land's coral beaches captivated me, and it was that allure that drew me to her. Additionally, she was the daughter of a soldier, and in my young mind, being a soldier's daughter was second only to being a soldier himself. This was around the time when, inspired by "The Story of the Hundred Days," I had set off with a satchel containing only a nightshirt and a toothbrush, hoping to enlist in the Black Watch. Alas, my quest ended rather abruptly at the train station. Ultimately, she bestowed upon me, as a symbol of her affection, "Poor Little Gaspard's Drum," a book that introduced me to Napoleon and the Egyptian desert, and most thrilling of all, the Mamelukes. Oh, how that word sent shivers down my spine! "The Mamelukes!" What could one do but fall for a girl who invoked such enchanting phrases?
