There is, of course, nothing inherently wrong with marrying for financial reasons. George Borrow once stated that there are worse avenues to wealth than marrying into it, and perhaps this holds some truth, though I find Borrow’s own experiences less than convincing. I have encountered individuals who pursued wealth and, in doing so, fell genuinely and passionately in love. However, it is essential to ensure that monetary gain is not the primary motive; otherwise, regret is sure to follow. Mr. Bumble married Mrs. Corney for "six teaspoons, a pair of sugar tongs, and a milk-pot, with a small quantity of secondhand furniture and twenty pounds in money." Just two months later, he lamented his decision, admitting he had gone "dirt cheap." "Only two months to-morrow," he mused, "It seems an age."

Those who subscribe to the notion of "love at first sight" believe that marriages are divinely orchestrated and that our earthly existence is merely about fulfilling that destiny. Johnson, who was a devoted husband to the elderly Mrs. Porter, scoffed at this belief, asserting that love is merely a product of circumstances. While this practical viewpoint is sensible, there are notable exceptions, such as the tales of Dante and Beatrice or Abelard and Heloise, where passion seems to ascend to the heavens. However, such relationships rarely conclude in happiness. A more mundane approach to love appears more suited to earthly realities.

Sir Thomas More's methods of courting were perhaps the most unusual on record. He had developed a preference for the second of three sisters and was poised to marry her when he experienced a moment of realization—But let me share the words of Roper, his son-in-law, who documented the event:

"And all beit his mynde most served him to the seconde daughter, for that he thoughte her the fayrest and best favoured, yet when he considered that it woulde be bothe great griefe and some shame alsoe to the eldest to see her yonger sister in mariage preferred before her, he then of a certeyn pittye framed his fancye towardes her, and soon after maryed her."

This illustrates a calculated form of love, yet it resulted in one of the most beautiful family lives imaginable, centered around this remarkable figure of English heritage.

In conclusion, there exists no universal formula for falling in love. Each individual embarks on that journey guided by their own spirit and circumstances.

In August, there's a certain pleasure in relaxing in Fleet Street or wherever the demands of work may confine you, while reminiscing about the sea. I find no envy for the throngs flocking to Margate and Blackpool, Salcombe and Minehead, for I've convinced myself that the sea has lost its charm since my youth. Back then, the tidal pools brimmed with starfish, sizable crabs roamed the empty shores, and anemones danced with their tentacles from every crevice.

While poets may claim the sea remains unchanged (and they might be correct regarding the water itself), I suspect the beaches are deteriorating. Over the past decade, I doubt I’ve encountered more than five starfish, despite numerous walks along the shoreline—not solely in pursuit of lost golf balls. Occasionally, I might spot a small crab hastily retreating to safety, but the formidable creatures that once sparked both fear and excitement during our childhood escapades are conspicuously absent. I cannot accept the rationale that my finger has simply grown larger; I would prefer to believe that today's children discover crabs and starfish in the same abundance and size I once did. Yet, we cannot ignore the fact that their numbers are dwindling. It’s clear that repeatedly collecting starfish to display as barometers in our homes detracts from the future generations' experience.

Another pastime of our youth, I suppose, has become inaccessible to children today. We would wait for the tide to recede just enough before daring to traverse the base of the cliffs, moving from one sandy cove to another. The waves would lap at the rocks, and a single misstep could send us tumbling into the water. It was thrilling to feel the peril of being caught by the rising tide without facing actual danger. On rare occasions, we were fortunate enough to see frantic figures at the cliff's summit, ignorant of the true nature of our adventure, believing we were in dire straits. Those moments were particularly exhilarating.

My friend once declared that it was his fate to acquire items from the most expensive markets and to sell them—if he managed to sell at all—at the lowest prices. More often than not, after tiring of a piece of art or a decorative item, I found myself compelled to give it away, almost pleading with others to accept it as a personal favor. Yet, an incident occurred recently that deviated so significantly from this pattern that I began to wonder if perhaps my fortunes had shifted, allowing me to become a truly enviable figure—a successful dealer.

The event unfolded during one of my meandering explorations through the quaint curiosity shops in a cathedral city. There, I stumbled across a portfolio filled with watercolor drawings, one of which caught my eye. It bore an uncanny resemblance to the work of Turner, a notion seemingly shared by a previous owner who had inscribed the esteemed artist's name—albeit with the initials jumbled—beneath the artwork.

Curiosity piqued, I inquired, “How much for this?”

The dealer responded, “Well, if it were a genuine Turner, it could command any price. But let’s settle on ten shillings for now. You can have it for that amount, though I won’t mind if you pass; I plan to take it to London next week to seek a professional opinion.”

I considered his words carefully.

“Now, I don’t guarantee its authenticity,” he added.

Without further hesitation, I handed over the ten shillings.

The details of how I ultimately found a buyer willing to pay fifty pounds for that drawing are not the focus of this tale. What truly matters is the internal negotiation I faced. The astonishing reality was that I had made a profit of forty-nine pounds ten shillings, which filled me with elation. However, this newfound success prompted deeper reflections.

As my eyes took in these fleeting impressions and my mind processed these superficial judgments, a deeper, almost primal sense of pity and fear stirred within me—an emotion that has eluded articulation since the dawn of humanity and serves as the driving force behind much of the world’s poetry. This mood is difficult to express, yet it can be faintly captured by the notion that tragedy is the ultimate testament to the profound value of human existence. I had never been so close to suffering and yet so distant from despair. Ordinarily, I would refrain from discussing such dark emotions, as they are challenging to convey; however, I feel compelled to mention them now for a particular reason, which I will outline shortly. These feelings led me to a unique realization concerning a social and political truth. It became vividly clear to me what the essence of a jury is and why it must never be allowed to perish.

Our contemporary era has been characterized by a relentless movement toward specialization and professionalism. We have trained soldiers who fight more effectively, singers who hit the right notes, dancers who captivate audiences, and even specialized laughers who bring joy more skillfully. This principle has been extended to the realms of law and politics, as many modern writers have pointed out. Numerous Fabians advocate for a significant portion of our political endeavors to be handled by experts, while various legal theorists argue for the complete replacement of untrained juries with trained judges.

If our world were genuinely rational, there might be no real objections to this trend. However, the true outcome of all experience and the foundation of all religious thought reveal another truth: the few essential things a person ought to grasp are paradoxical in nature. That is, although we recognize these truths as self-evident in life, articulating them often leads to apparent contradictions. For example, it is a well-known yet paradoxical truth that those who seek pleasure the most often find it elusive. Another paradox lies in the concept of courage; the idea that fearing death too intensely can ironically lead to its greater likelihood. Those who dare to climb a perilous cliff may, through their very recklessness, escape injury. The adage “whoever will lose his life shall save it” embodies this practical truth.

The Fabian claim, which suggests that expertise should drive trust, would be irrefutable if it were true that those who immerse themselves in a subject gradually uncover its deeper significance. In reality, the opposite often occurs; as one studies intensely, they may lose sight of the very essence they initially sought to grasp. This phenomenon affects us all, as we often drift away from appreciating the significance of the sky or the stones around us unless we actively cultivate a sense of gratitude and humility.

It is a grave matter to single out an individual for the wrath of society. Yet, like many terrible realities, one can become accustomed to it, much like one can acclimatize to the sun's glare. They do not see the gravity of the court as it truly is; they merely recognize their workplace. Ordinary citizens must be brought in, individuals who can truly see the court, the crowd, the rough features of the police, the faces of the accused, and the rehearsed expressions of counsel, experiencing it all as one would a new painting or an unfamiliar performance.

Our society has justly resolved that deciding the guilt or innocence of individuals is too crucial a matter to be entrusted solely to trained professionals. When the task at hand involves cataloging a library or exploring the solar system, specialists are employed. I have yet to encounter a narrative about the war that resonates with me as deeply as the account Mr. Alfred Noyes shared in the newspapers regarding his visit to the Fleet. This tale centers on the Battle of Jutland. "In the very hottest moment of this most stupendous battle in all history," he recounts, "two grimy stokers' heads arose for a breath of fresh air. What domestic drama they were discussing the world may never know. But the words that were actually heard passing between them, while the shells whined overhead, were these: 'What I says is, 'e ought to have married 'er.'"

If you find this story unappealing, you will struggle to grasp the essence of the English spirit. Some individuals among us may never truly understand it. In the war's early days, a close friend of mine was deeply troubled by the song "Tipperary." He questioned how a nation could send its soldiers into battle singing "Tipperary" when their opponents marched forward chanting "Ein' feste Burg." Framed in that manner, I had to concede that the situation appeared grim for us. It seemed "all Lombard Street to a China orange," as an old saying goes. While "Tipperary" was somewhat refreshing and original for a music-hall tune, it stood in stark contrast to the sentimental "Keep the home fires burning," which dominates today’s landscape. I still experience a bittersweet pleasure whenever I hear it on a street organ; its joyful melody is inevitably intertwined with the profound emotions of those unforgettable days, much like a butterfly caught in a tempest.

Yet, in the end, it was merely a music-hall tune, and comparing it to Luther’s powerful hymn would be akin to pitting a pop-gun against a formidable artillery piece. The resonance of Luther's hymn has echoed through four centuries and will continue to reverberate through time until the end of days. It embodies the epic clash of elements, akin to the rumble of mountains and the swell of oceans. Nowhere else is the embodiment of Power so vividly expressed in song. The lyrics are just as formidable as the melody. Carlyle captured their raw, robust strength in his renowned translation:

A safe stronghold our God is still, A trusty shield and weapon; He'll help us clear from all the ill That hath us now o'ertaken….

On my final morning along the Flemish coastline, with the knowledge that I would soon be crossing over to England, my attention was caught by a piece of Gothic carving, a common sight in Flanders. Its age was uncertain, as it bore the marks of wear and was somewhat illegible, yet it undeniably reflected the style of the early Middle Ages. The sculpture seemed to depict individuals engaged in various primary activities: some appeared to be sailors tugging on ropes, others were reaping crops, and a few were energetically pouring substances into each other. This portrayal is emblematic of the early thirteenth century, a period renowned for its vigorous spirit. In contrast, the ancient Greeks tended to immortalize their gods and heroes in moments of stillness. Their art, while splendid and philosophical in its poise, often conveyed a sense of detachment, as if they were masters presiding over a multitude of laborers. In stark contrast, the early medieval artists relished the representation of people in action—be it hunting, boating, grape treading, shoemaking, or cooking. The essence of life was captured in their works, showcasing the vibrancy of human endeavor. The Middle Ages, a time of burgeoning social order, was marked by strong religious convictions that had yet to become burdensome. This distinct contrast between Greek and Gothic art is palpable; the figures of the Elgin marbles appear eternally frozen in a moment of perfection, while medieval carvings emanate a sense of movement and activity, akin to the buzz of a beehive surrounding a grand cathedral.

However, there was something peculiar about these particular figures that left me uncertain. Those that had heads bore oddly shaped features, and it seemed to me that their mouths were open. I couldn’t tell if this was a deliberate artistic choice or merely an artifact of nascent creativity. As I pondered this, I recalled how singing was often intertwined with many of the tasks depicted—there are songs for reapers and for sailors hauling ropes. My thoughts continued to wander while I strolled along the pier at Ostend, where I heard sailors shouting in rhythm as they worked. This reminded me that sailors still chant in unison while laboring, often changing their songs based on the specific tasks at hand. Later, after my sea journey concluded, the sight of men toiling in English fields brought to mind the traditional songs associated with harvesting and various agricultural activities. It struck me as curious that, despite this rich history, no modern trades seem to possess a ritualistic form of poetry. How did it come to be that people sang simple verses while performing specific tasks like pulling ropes or gathering fruit? Why is it that no one engages in similar practices while creating modern products? It is unusual that a contemporary newspaper is never printed with the accompaniment of a chorus, nor do shopkeepers ever seem to break into song.

Among the various columns in newspapers, one that consistently captures my interest—always excluding those I contribute to myself—is the section called "The World's Press." This feature offers a glimpse into the perspectives of publications that often fly under the radar for most readers. Recently, I stumbled upon The Shoe Manufacturers' Monthly, a periodical that the discerning crowd eagerly anticipates each month. Its former competitor, The Footwear Fortnightly, seems to have faded from relevance. One amusing tidbit from the latest edition notes that Kaffirs have a peculiar preference for boots that make noise. I mention this as a pretext to delve into the age-old conundrum of squeaky boots and collars, essentially highlighting the inherent unfairness of life.

Those well-versed in fashion—especially the majors and clubmen who regularly dispense advice on attire—have attempted to elucidate the reasons behind a squeaky collar. However, their explanations rarely satisfy anyone with a modicum of intelligence. They attribute the issue to a collar being either too large or too small, excessively dirty or overly clean. They contend that if one has collars tailored to fit (like a true gentleman), all will be well, whereas purchasing cheap, off-the-rack options is the root of the problem. They propose using a bit of soap on the outside of the shirt or suggesting various remedies, but they are fundamentally mistaken.

The straightforward reality, which most people recognize, is that some individuals are simply more prone to having squeaky collars than others. A collar that squeaks on a man is less a commentary on the collar itself and more a reflection of the man wearing it. He is, in essence, unlucky. Despite whatever advantages nature may have bestowed upon him—handsome looks or a noble character—he finds himself at odds with the inanimate objects around him.

The postman has just left, and among the letters he delivered was one from North Wales. It was plump and soft, and upon opening it, we discovered it contained a piece of seaweed. While the sender's intention was warm and friendly, the immediate effect was to awaken intense yearnings for the sea, which only deepened our grievances against the Kaiser, who had forced us to spend our holiday in the countryside—where we were compelled to economize—rather than at the beach, where the allure of indulgence would be irresistible. “Ah, it smells like Sheringham,” declared one person, whose loyalty lies with the East Coast. “No, this has the scent of Sidmouth, Dawlish, and Torquay,” countered another, who is enamored with the red cliffs of South Devon. The conversation continued as each individual inhaled the aroma of the seaweed, allowing their memories to cascade forth, revealing a panorama of summer sea experiences. The table soon became awash with a deluge of nostalgia—thoughts of swimming and sailing, of racing barefoot on the beach, of cheerful fishermen eternally gazing out to sea for an elusive catch, of shell hunting, and of the carefree joys encountered at dawn, noon, and dusk by the shore. All of this was stirred by merely the scent of a piece of seaweed.

This enchanting power of remembrance transforms our world into a treasure chest of personal histories and secrets. Few are the birds that sing, flowers that bloom, or clouds that drift across the azure sky that do not evoke some memory from the past, stirring us with recollection. A chance encounter with an open drawer releases the fragrance of lavender, and with that evocative scent, the past unfurls like a scroll, bringing to life places long forgotten and voices long silent:

We walk along the path they have trodden. We take our seats beneath their orchard's shade, We listen, as they did, to the drone of bees, And the rustling of the corn in the breeze.

Their vibrant blooms are imbued with the memories of every spring that has come before and the promise of those yet to arrive. They connect us to nature’s grand pageant and to the enduring spirits of our literary forebears—Wordsworth, who watched them dance merrily by Ullswater, Herrick, who found in them a poignant symbol of life's fleeting beauty, and Shakespeare, who welcomed them "in the sweet o' the year" beside the banks of the Avon centuries ago.

In this sensitivity of memory to external stimuli lies an infinite spectrum of responses. It is not a collective recollection that is stirred, but rather a deeply personal one. That fragment of seaweed opened numerous windows within us, each leading to unique vistas and triggering distinct, inexplicable feelings—moments that embody the innate solitude we all experience. Every item speaks a private dialect to us, one that we can never fully translate for others. I cannot say what the lilac conveys to you; for me, it conjures an image of a garden gate that once stood long ago. I become a child again, standing at that gate, where I can see red-coated soldiers marching by, laughing and snatching lilac blooms as they pass. The pride I felt, knowing that these heroes took the time to appreciate our lilac tree, floods back to me, intertwined with memories of the old garden, the home of my youth, and faces that have long since faded. Why that fleeting image has remained etched in my memory, I cannot explain, yet it persists, as vivid and clear nearly fifty years later as if it were painted just yesterday, and the blooming lilac tree always brings it back to life.

We’ve all encountered individuals who recount strange occurrences with a skeptical tone, insisting that despite the oddities, they do not believe in the supernatural. In stark contrast, I find myself firmly grounded in the belief of the supernatural, rooted in intellect and reason rather than personal encounters. I don’t perceive ghosts; instead, I recognize their intrinsic likelihood. My understanding is purely cerebral; my physical being is firmly tethered to this world. Yet, it is often the most peculiar experiences that leave a lasting impression on those of my mindset. The most bizarre event I have ever encountered unfolded recently, centering around my ability to engage in a game—one that I played surprisingly well for a solid seventeen minutes. I daresay, even the ghost of my grandfather would have evoked less astonishment.

On one of those brilliant, scorching afternoons, I found myself, to my utter disbelief, participating in a game of croquet. I had always assumed this pastime was a relic of the days of Leach and Anthony Trollope, and thus I had neglected to don the extravagant side whiskers that seem essential for such an occasion. I played alongside a man I shall refer to as Parkinson; our match was accompanied by a semi-philosophical debate that persisted throughout the duration of the game. I am convinced that I held the upper hand in our discussions, yet it is undeniable that I was thoroughly outmatched in the game itself.

“Oh, Parkinson, Parkinson!” I exclaimed, affectionately tapping him on the head with my mallet. “You are so far removed from the pure love of the sport! You, who can actually play! It is we, the inept, who find joy in the essence of the game. You crave glory; you seek the thunderous applause of victory; you do not truly love croquet. You cannot profess your love for the game until you have embraced the possibility of defeat in croquet. It is we, the bunglers, who worship the sport for its own sake. If we could glimpse the face of Croquet herself—if I may put it that way—we would be content to see her expression of displeasure. Our play is labeled as amateurish, yet we wear that title with pride, for 'amateur' derives from the French word for 'lover.' We accept all the encounters she offers, whether they lead to disaster or monotony. We linger outside her iron gates—those hoops, if you will—striving to gain entry. Our devoted balls, eager and chivalrous, refuse to be confined within the rigid confines of the croquet lawn. They seek honor in the far reaches of the earth; they end up in flower beds, conservatories, front gardens, and even in neighboring streets. No, Parkinson! A skilled painter possesses technique; it is the unskilled painter who cherishes his art. A proficient musician revels in his craft, while the mediocre musician loves music itself. With a pure and unrelenting passion, I revere croquet. I adore the game for its own sake. I cherish the rectangular patch of grass outlined by chalk or tape, as if its boundaries represent the frontiers of my sacred homeland, the four seas of Britain. I delight in the simple swing of the mallet, while the sound of the balls colliding is like music to my ears. The four colors resonate deeply with me, each symbolizing something profound, akin to the red of martyrdom or the white of Easter Sunday. You miss all of this, dear Parkinson. To comfort yourself for the absence of this vision, you resort to the trivial consolation of successfully navigating hoops and striking the stick.”

With that, I flourished my mallet with a lighthearted elegance.

“Don’t lament my fate too much,” Parkinson replied, his tone tinged with playful sarcasm. “I’ll recover from this in due time. However, it strikes me that the more one enjoys a game, the more one wishes to excel at it. While the pleasure derived from the activity itself is paramount, doesn’t the satisfaction of success naturally follow? Consider your own analogy of the Knight and his Lady-love. Admittedly, the gentleman’s foremost desire is to be in the presence of the lady. Yet, I’ve never heard of a gentleman who would want to appear foolish in her company.”

“Perhaps not; though he often ends up looking foolish,” I countered. “However, therein lies a flaw in the analogy, despite it being my own creation. The joy sought by the lover is a boundless happiness that can expand infinitely. Generally speaking, the more he is loved, the happier he becomes. It’s true that the deeper the love shared between both lovers, the greater the joy will be. Yet, it’s not the case that the better both croquet players perform, the more enjoyable the game becomes. It is entirely feasible—(stay with me here, Parkinson!)—to play croquet too well to actually derive pleasure from it. If you could send that blue ball through that distant hoop as easily as picking it up with your hand, you would not bother to do it; it would lose its significance. If you could play flawlessly, you would cease to play altogether. Once the game reaches perfection, it ceases to exist.”

“I don’t believe, however,” Parkinson interjected, “that you are in any immediate danger of achieving that level of perfection. I doubt your croquet will vanish due to its own excellence. You’re safe for now.”

Once again, I affectionately tapped him with the mallet, sent a ball flying, and picked up where I left off in our discussion.

As the long, warm evening gradually descended, twilight was settling in. By the time I articulated four more fundamental principles, and Parkinson managed to navigate five additional hoops, the encroaching darkness was almost complete.

“We’ll have to call it a night,” Parkinson said, missing a ball for what seemed like the first time. “I can’t see a thing.”

“Neither can I,” I replied, “and it’s somewhat comforting to recognize that I couldn’t hit anything even if I could see it.”

With that, I struck the ball decisively, sending it off into the darkness toward the hazy shape of Parkinson. He let out a loud and dramatic exclamation. The situation indeed warranted such a response, as I had struck the correct ball.

Astonished, I traversed the dimly lit ground and hit my ball again. It rolled through a hoop. I couldn’t see the hoop, but I was certain it was the right one. A shiver ran through my body.

Words escaped me, so I trudged heavily after that incredible ball. Once more, I struck it into the night, believing I was aiming in the general direction of another ball. In the oppressive silence, I heard the dull thud as the ball made contact with the stick.

I dropped my mallet, exclaiming, “I can’t endure this! My ball has gone through the hoop three times. These phenomena are not of this realm.”

“Pick up your mallet,” Parkinson urged, “and give it another try.”

“I refuse to. If I were to accomplish another hoop like that, I’d be confronted by a legion of devils dancing on the blessed grass.”

“Why devils?” Parkinson questioned. “They could be merely fairies having their fun. They’re bestowing upon you the ‘Perfect Game,’ which is no game at all.”

I glanced around, the garden enveloped in an intense darkness, where the faint glimmers appeared almost like flames. I stepped gingerly across the grass, as though it were on fire, retrieved the mallet, and struck the ball somewhere—anywhere another ball might be. I heard the dull clack of the balls colliding and dashed into the house as if I were being pursued.

In an American publication, I came across an amusing anecdote: "An elderly woman was being guided to the location where a hero met his demise. 'I’m not surprised,' she responded. 'It's so slippery that I almost fell myself.'"

This tale, which has long been part of English folklore, is commonly associated with Nelson and his ship, the Victory. It has become such a well-known quip amongst playful tourists visiting that vessel that the more astute guides make it a point to mention it first. Yet in America, this story may still hold a certain novelty and could very well begin a new chapter in its life. It is likely to persist indefinitely in English-speaking regions, reviving with each retelling and finding fresh audiences who encounter it for the first time.

It raises an interesting question as to why we often feel irked when an editor or comedian presents us with a joke that has been recycled. This irritation seems to stem, at least in part, from the fact that we have invested our money—whether for the newspaper or the ticket to a performance—and thus, we feel cheated. We believe we are purchasing a fresh and original experience, so when confronted with an old and perhaps even familiar joke—one we might have told ourselves—it heightens our indignation. One wonders, however, what a comedic publication or show devoid of any old material would even resemble. That remains a mystery.

We also resent the laughter of those in the audience who are hearing it for the first time—perhaps three-quarters of the crowd. Engaged in a contest of memory with another performer, he concluded the debate with the claim that he could remember London Bridge when it was merely a cornfield. This notion may not be comforting to those who prefer their humor to possess a certain antiquity, but it is a reality grounded in nature. Just as I was once told by a solemn nurse that a child is born every moment (she added, with a finger raised for emphasis, that someone also dies in that same instant), so too is an older child reaching an age where they can appreciate and understand humor nearly every moment. To these children, every story feels original. With this fresh audience, eager and appreciative, one wonders why humorists strive so diligently for novelty. Though perhaps they do not.

There are likely various theories regarding the oldest jokes in existence, yet I am unfamiliar with them. What is evident, however, is that people are inherently prepared for every story to be old, as demonstrated by how readily audiences noted when Mark Twain’s “Jumping Frog” was translated into Greek for a school reader. Many remarked that Twain had drawn from ancient literature for his humor. This peculiar tendency reveals our collective desire for stories to possess a sense of familiarity. While we do enjoy a new tale, we often value even more the ability to claim that it resonates with us as something we have encountered before.

Certain stories seem to resurface periodically, particularly those with a military context. For instance, during the Great War, anecdotes featuring such themes reemerged. I recall hearing during the Boer War about a young man who was turned away from enlisting due to dental issues. “But I want to fight the Boers,” he protested, “not eat them.” This clever retort resurfaced between 1914 and 1918, but this time, the young man insisted he did not wish to consume the Germans. I am certain that a similar narrative found its way into the accounts of the Crimean War, where another recruit claimed he did not want to eat the Russians, and a century earlier, someone was asserting the same about the French. In fact, it is likely that this theme could be traced through every conflict in history. Perhaps a young Hittite with poor dental health proclaimed a desire to battle the Amalekites rather than feast upon them. Each iteration of this story remains equally effective, and there has always been a vast new audience ready to appreciate it. As long as warfare persists and humans retain teeth—an assertion I’ve heard might not hold forever—this anecdote will remain popular. Eventually, it may transition into a different narrative phase based on other deficiencies in the recruit's dental health, and this cycle will continue until universal peace reigns or, as some predict, life itself comes to an end with the cooling of the sun.

The other day, I set off from Keswick, a rucksack slung over my shoulders, a Baddeley guide tucked into my pocket, and a companion accompanying me. Walking with a partner adds to the experience; as Sterne once expressed, "Give me a companion by the way," even if it’s just to notice how shadows stretch as the sun dips lower. That’s about all the conversation one needs. Engaging in chatter at the outset is fine, but as the journey progresses and you become absorbed in the task at hand, silence becomes more appealing. Often, you may find yourselves trailing one another, saving your discussions for the inn later and the comfort of a post-dinner pipe. A shared laugh, a spontaneous song, or a brief review of the map is more than sufficient for the trail.

At the head of Derwentwater, we boarded a boat and glided across the lake to the small bay nestled at the base of Catbells. We disembarked, adjusted our packs, and embarked on our journey over the mountains and through the passes, relishing a week immersed in the profound solitude that this region has to offer. We didn’t adhere to a strict itinerary. While I enjoy creating plans for hiking expeditions, I find even greater joy in deviating from them. The freedom that walking imparts is one of its greatest pleasures. You are not bound by schedules, nor confined to a specific route, nor beholden to anyone. If a particular path captures your interest, you can follow it; if you prefer a different pass, it’s yours to choose; and if the allure of the mountain peaks calls to you, then over Great Gable and Scafell, Robinson and Helvellyn you shall traverse. Every shortcut beckons, every trail offers a chance for adventure. The stream cascading down the mountainside becomes your cup of wine. Kneeling on the stones, you lean down to drink from it, savoring the refreshment that only the mountains can provide. Then, with a renewed spirit, you continue on your way, singing:

Bed in the bush with the stars to see. Bread I dip in the river— There's the life for a man like me. There's the life for ever.

What other freedom compares? You have severed your ties with the world, distancing yourself from telegraphs, newspapers, and the chaos of the life you’ve left behind. You stand alone among the solitary hills, beneath an expansive sky, surrounded by the elemental forces that have existed since time immemorial and will endure long after the tumult of humanity fades away. The sounds of life—the curlew’s whistle, the bleating of sheep—only deepen the sense of ancient isolation. These echoes have resonated off the crags for millennia; their harmonies, alongside the rush of winds and waters, will continue to reverberate for countless more years. It feels like you have transcended time, entering a realm where a thousand years is but a fleeting moment. Here, there’s no calendar to dictate your existence. The buzzard, startled from its perch in a gully, circles above with wings spread wide, tracing a lineage as old as the mountains themselves. The breathtaking view of the Langdale peaks, which greets you as you reach the summit of Esk Hause, is the same sight that greeted the first intrepid soul who ventured into these wild mountain fastnesses.

As the sun tilts toward the horizon, reality sets in. You are reminded that, while surrounded by eternal wonders, you are still very much mortal, feeling the fatigue in your feet and realizing the need for rest and refuge for the night. Where shall we go? The valleys beckon from all directions. We could head toward the expansive Newlands Vale, the cheerful Borrowdale, the serene Ennerdale, or—yes, tonight we’ll dine at Wastdale, at the cheerful old inn once run by Auld Will Ritson, a sanctuary for cragsmen. It’s a place where, on New Year’s Eve, climbers gather to share stories of their mountain exploits, discussing handholds and footholds, joining in the lively chorus of “The rope, the rope,” led by the landlord who heartily sings:

I'm not a climber, not a climber, Not a climber now, My weight is going fourteen stone— I'm not a climber now.

Tonight, we won’t see Gaspard—the spirited and fearless guide from the Dauphiné, a favorite among those who frequent the lonely inn at Wastdale. He’s off fighting a more formidable enemy than the rocky heights of Great Gable and Scafell. However, Old Joe, the shepherd, will be there—Old Joe, who has never traveled by train or set foot in a town, renowned for his ability to pull the ugliest faces in all of Cumberland. He reserves them for moments of good cheer and for his friends in the back parlor. Perhaps tonight, we will witness his eyes rolling as he passionately belts out the chorus of “D’ye ken John Peel?” Yes, Wastdale will be our stop for the night. Thus, we will traverse Black Sail and descend the rugged mountainside to the inn, its whitewashed walls greeting us from the encroaching shadows of the valley.

Moreover, the number of appointments I had where others did not show up forced me to reevaluate my stance. The disarray this caused was particularly frustrating during a time when I was feeling exceptionally busy. Additionally, I found that waiting for someone who was late left me feeling restless and unable to focus on anything else.

After all, one often hears about the precision associated with the Army, and my most punctual friend had been a soldier, which sparked a friendly rivalry between us. However, my expectations were dashed. Soldiers on leave exploited the goodwill of those they visited, and the first demobilized soldier I hosted kept me waiting for dinner a full forty minutes.

In a quiet corner of a London club, a small assembly of men, each of whom had achieved remarkable success in their respective fields, gathered around the fireplace after a dinner. This group comprised a distinguished lawyer, a renowned politician, a prominent clergyman, and a seasoned journalist. As their conversation meandered through various topics, it inevitably landed on a familiar question: If given the chance, would you choose to relive your life? With one notable exception, the consensus was a resounding "No." Interestingly, the exception was not the clergyman. He, like the others, felt that a single experience of life was sufficient and had no desire to revisit it.

This inquiry, I suspect, is as ancient as humanity itself. The response is equally timeless, often mirroring that of our gathered company by the fire. This question typically arises in midlife, as youthful exuberance tends to overlook such contemplations. In our younger years, life unfolds like an endless horizon, rendering the notion of its recurrence irrelevant. It is only when we reach the peak of our journey, beginning to descend with the evening shadows casting long over the valley, that this question emerges unbidden. The answer does not imply that the journey was unworthy; rather, it signifies the weariness of the path traveled. We find ourselves exhausted, longing for rest, and it serves as nature’s way of reconciling us with our mortality. Life has shown us its grand spectacle, and now it prepares us for our inevitable return to the earth.

Indeed, we come to accept the finality of life without complaint, even if offered the chance to turn back time, we would likely decline.

However, this contemplation should not be confused with the more frivolous inquiry: "Is life worth living?" The men in the smoking-room would have responded to that question with an immediate and dismissive "Yes." Each had experienced life as a magnificent adventure, making the most of their time and cherishing every moment of its rich tapestry. This sentiment is true for all who possess a healthy mindset. In our darker moments, we might echo Job and lament our birth, yet such curses quickly fade. Swift, despite his mourning of his own birthday, could not truly despise life, for to loathe humanity would render existence unbearable. The depth of our sympathies directly correlates with our joy in living.

Recently, I experienced a moment of sheer surprise when I managed to catch a train heading towards the Eastern Counties. I barely made it, and while I hurried alongside the train, I became aware of an unusually high number of carriages labeled "Engaged." The notices were visible on five, six, seven, or even eight carriages, with large, imposing men gazing out from the windows, their expressions reflecting a peculiar pride. Their demeanor seemed especially impenetrable, and their faces wore an unusual calmness. It was not Derby Day, as the train was headed in the opposite direction and it was not the appropriate time. It couldn't be the King or the French President either. While such prominent figures typically enjoy privacy during their travels, they also attract crowds and police presence when they board a train. Yet, here there was neither a gathering of onlookers nor any ceremonial security.

Who were these formidable individuals occupying a substantial portion of the train, outnumbering a gathering of revelers yet exhibiting a peculiar delicacy that seemed more fitting for the royal entourage? Was it conceivable that rather than the Royal Family visiting the Tsar, the Tsar was actually visiting us? Or perhaps there was a breakfast gathering of the House of Lords? My curiosity deepened as the train slowed at a station en route to Cambridge. The large, inscrutable men disembarked, followed by their distinguished companions, each of whom appeared to be dressed uniformly, with neatly cropped hair and a peculiar chain linking them together.

Across the carriage, I made eye contact with the only other passenger. He was a small, weary-looking man, who I later learned hailed from Cambridge. Judging by his appearance, he seemed to be a local tradesman, perhaps a journeyman tailor or a clock mender. In an effort to strike up a conversation, I expressed my curiosity about where the convicts might be headed. His mouth twitched in a wry smile, hinting at the irony that often accompanies the plight of the common man, and he replied, “I don’t suppose they’re goin’ on an ’oliday at the seaside with little spades and pails.” I found his humor delightful and continued to play along, suggesting that maybe academics were being escorted to Cambridge in similar chains. As someone familiar with the dons, he found this notion amusing. However, our laughter soon gave way to a somber silence, and I noticed a profound sadness in his bleak, gray eyes, which seemed emptier than the vast ocean. I understood his thoughts mirrored my own; despite our attempts at humor, we both recognized the underlying seriousness of our reality. Eventually, he broke the silence with, “Well, I s’pose we ’ave to do it.” In his initial jest, his silence, and his concluding remark lay the essence of three fundamental truths about English democracy: a deep sense of humor, a poignant sense of pathos, and a pervasive sense of helplessness.

The challenge in addressing the issue of how to treat criminals with decency lies in the detachment exhibited by both sides of the argument. Those who condemn wrongdoing often approach the subject with as much coldness as those who orchestrate it. Humanitarianism can sometimes be as harsh as inhumanity itself.

The cat-o'-nine-tails is merely a modern version of the rack, stripped of any intellectual justification. Historically, torture has thrived alongside the most sophisticated cultures, reaching its peak in artistic expressions during the late Roman Empire, the ornate sixteenth century, the centralized French monarchy before the Revolution, and continues to exist in refined forms within certain modern societies. This is a sobering realization we must confront. As we become more educated and refined, we must recognize that we are not inevitably moving away from the specter of torture. Over a month ago, as I prepared to depart from London for a vacation, a friend entered my Battersea flat and observed my chaotic packing.

“You seem to be heading off somewhere,” he remarked. “Where are you headed?”

With a strap clenched between my teeth, I managed to respond, “To Battersea.”

“The cleverness of your statement is lost on me,” he replied.

“I am indeed going to Battersea,” I clarified, “but via Paris, Belfort, Heidelberg, and Frankfurt. My remark holds no humor; it is simply a fact. I intend to traverse the globe until I rediscover Battersea. Somewhere amidst the seas of dawn or dusk, in the farthest reaches of the earth, lies a small isle that I aim to uncover: one adorned with gentle green hills and towering white cliffs. Travelers inform me that it is known as England (while Scottish travelers assert it is called Britain), and I have heard whispers that at its core lies a lovely place called Battersea.”

“I guess it’s unnecessary to remind you,” my friend said, with an air of superiority, “that this is Battersea?”

“Unnecessary indeed,” I replied, “and it lacks spiritual truth. I cannot perceive any Battersea here; neither can I discern London or England. I cannot even see that door or that chair; a veil of drowsiness and familiarity has clouded my vision. The only path back to clarity is to venture elsewhere. That is the essence of travel and the joy of holidays. Do you think I travel to France merely to see France? I will certainly enjoy both countries, but they are not my destination. My quest is to find Battersea. The true purpose of travel is not to step onto foreign soil; it is ultimately to return to one’s own homeland as if it were foreign. I must warn you, though, this Gladstone bag is quite heavy, and should you utter the word ‘paradox,’ I might just throw it at you. I didn’t create this world, nor did I make it paradoxical. It’s not my fault, but rather the truth, that the only route back to England involves departing from it.”

England greeted me as both stunningly new and beautifully familiar. Arriving at Dover is indeed the ideal way to enter England, as it allows one to first behold the lush, gentle gardens of Kent, which, while perhaps exaggerated, still typify the rich rustic charm of the country. Coincidentally, I struck up a conversation with a fellow traveler, an American lady who had explored Europe but had yet to set foot in England. Her enthusiasm was expressed in that straightforward, exuberant manner typical of Americans, who, in my view, are the most idealistic people on earth. Their only risk is that an idealist can easily slip into idolization. Indeed, the American idealism extends even to the glorification of wealth. “I’ve never been to England before,” the American lady said. “Yet it’s so beautiful that it feels like I’ve been away from it for ages.”

“I’m intrigued to hear your perspective,” I said. “I’m currently compiling a list of the things that are genuinely better in England. In fact, most of what the DAILY MAIL touts as English is notably superior elsewhere. But there are elements that are quintessentially English and undeniably good: kippers, Free Trade, front gardens, individual liberty, the Elizabethan drama, hansom cabs, cricket, and Mr. Will Crooks. As she admired the ivy, I picked up an English newspaper for the first time in weeks and read a speech by Mr. Balfour. He argued that the House of Lords should be preserved because it embodied a form of enduring public opinion in England, rising above the fluctuations of political parties. Mr. Balfour is a sincere patriot, a man who contemplates the public’s needs with considerable seriousness, and he possesses notable intellectual prowess. However, after reading his words, I felt a heavy sense of sadness as I realized I had to add yet another entry to my list of uniquely English phenomena: the distinctively English variety of humbug. In France, things are critiqued and defended based on their true nature. The Catholic Church is criticized for being Catholic and defended for the same reason. The Republic is supported because it is Republican and attacked for the very same reasons. Yet here we have one of England's most capable politicians assuring everyone that the House of Lords is not really what it seems, but something entirely different; that the foolish accidental peers he encounters each evening somehow possess insight into the psyche of the masses. If you wish to understand what the impoverished desire, he suggests, you must consult the wealthy, and if you seek the truth about Hoxton, you ought to inquire at Hatfield. If a Conservative defender of the House of Lords were a logical French politician, he would simply be a deceiver. However, in the realm of English politics, he becomes a poet. In a cold, logical sense, Mr. Balfour is aware that most Lords who aren’t titled by accident have acquired their status through bribery. Ultimately, he earnestly invites the English people to join him in venerating a noble and public-spirited Senate, having entirely forgotten that this Senate is, in fact, populated by individuals he himself has scorned and adventurers he has ennobled.

“Your ivy is so wonderfully soft and thick,” the American lady observed. “It seems to cover nearly everything. It must be the most poetic aspect of England.”

“It is indeed beautiful,” I replied, “and, as you noted, it is very much part of England. Let us appreciate the ivy; and let us fervently pray to God that it does not strangle the tree.”

A friend of mine, someone who knows me well enough to sense my hidden thoughts, recently posed an intriguing question: "Have you ever encountered 'Alpha of the Plough?'"

"I’ve never met him," I replied without hesitation, feeling quite unabashed. We both chuckled at the exchange.

"Really? Never at all?" he pressed.

"Not once," I confirmed. "And I can assure you, I never will."

"Not even in the mirror?" he quipped.

"That’s not really 'Alpha of the Plough,'" I countered. "That’s merely a facsimile. It could be a convincing imitation, but it’s not the actual person. I can perceive fragments of him—his hands, feet, and arms. By closing one eye, I can deduce the outline of his nose. If I push out my upper lip, I might notice he has a moustache. However, the entirety of his face remains concealed from me. I cannot describe even with the aid of the imitation what impression he leaves on those who observe him. Now," I paused to assess my friend thoughtfully, "I can gauge what you are like. I can take you in at a glance, and you can do the same with me. Yet, the one person we cannot perceive in entirety is the very individual we most desire to understand."

"That's a bit of a blessing," he remarked.

I’m not entirely convinced he was correct. In this intricate world, there are compelling arguments on both sides. It might be fortunate for some of us to remain perpetual strangers to ourselves, not just in our physical forms. We lack even the awareness of our own voices. Mr. Pemberton-Billing has never experienced the sound of his own deep voice in the House of Commons, while Lord Charles Beresford is oblivious to how a foghorn sounds when it articulates. You and I cannot fathom the impression our demeanor leaves on others. If we did, many of us would likely be devastated. The truth might be so shocking that we would wish we had never been born at all.

Consider, for instance, the distinguished politician Mr. Sutherland Bangs, M.P., encountering himself at a dinner party one evening. Mr. Sutherland Bangs harbors a pleasant self-image, envisioning himself as a charming, eloquent fellow, skilled in conversation, exuding a carefree nature, with a fashionable appearance and a refined accent. However, seated next to his own self at dinner, he would realize that he is, in fact, a pretentious bore, that his conversation is filled with banalities, his breezy demeanor grating, and his elegant accent nothing more than an annoying affectation. He would vow never to want to see that version of himself again. Returning home, he would feel as humbled and degraded as Mr. Tom Lofty in The Good-Natured Man when his true nature was revealed. "You ought to have your head stuck in a pillory," Mr. Croaker admonished Mr. Lofty. "Stick it wherever you like," Mr. Lofty replied, "for, by the Lord, it makes a poor showing wherever it is." Mr. Sutherland Bangs would certainly resonate with that sentiment.

Yet, while encountering our true selves might bring some of us profound surprise and even discomfort, it would also serve many of us a beneficial purpose. Burns articulated this sentiment beautifully in his well-known lines:

"O wad some pow'r the giftie gie us  
To see oursels as others see us:  
It wad frae monie a blunder free us  
An' foolish notion."

We would each uncover truths that could work to our advantage alongside our dismay. You, for instance, might discover that the argumentative prowess you take pride in is merely perceived by me as irritating obstinacy, while I might learn that the clever wit I believe I exhibit causes you fatigue. Jones might find his eyeglass falling from his eye, realizing it serves only to make him look foolish. Brown would confront the unattractiveness of his cant, and Robinson would regret his bullying nature and prickly demeanor. Gaining this objective perspective on ourselves would undoubtedly be beneficial.

However, this view isn’t necessarily the definitive or complete perspective. Recall Sherlock Holmes’ clever notion about John and Thomas. When they converse and struggle to connect, Holmes observes that it’s hardly surprising, considering that six identities are involved in the dialogue. "Six!" you might exclaim, surprised. Indeed, there are six: John’s ideal self—how he perceives himself; Thomas’s ideal view of John—how he sees John; and the real John, known solely to his Creator. The same applies to Thomas, who also embodies three different versions. The ideal self that John envisions is entirely dissimilar to how Thomas perceives him, and neither of these aligns with the authentic John, leading to a miscommunication between John and Thomas—that is, between you and me.

If I (John) could see myself through your (Thomas’s) eyes, observing my appearance, mannerisms, and behaviors, it would serve as a crucial corrective. It would cultivate the faculty of self-criticism that most of us lack. This ability is simply the skill to observe ourselves from an outsider’s perspective, devoid of bias and interest. Few possess this capability, except perhaps in fleeting moments of clarity. We struggle to apply it even to our creations. When you paint, write, or craft a joke, you can be certain that you will likely misjudge its quality. You perceive it subjectively as part of your identity, which means you don’t truly see it. If you set it aside for a year and then encounter it unexpectedly, much like a stranger would, you may finally grasp why Thomas appeared unfazed. It wasn’t due to jealousy or hostility, as you once assumed; rather, he perceived it clearly while you could not.

Even the most notable figures can fall prey to this blindness regarding their own work. This phenomenon is evident in the case of Wordsworth. He stands among the three greatest poets this country has ever produced and was also a discerning critic of poetry. Yet, he authored more pedestrian prose than any of his contemporaries. He seemed oblivious to when his writing reached sublime heights and when it descended into mere drivel. This lack of awareness stemmed from his inability to step outside the self-induced trance of his own perception.

I beheld its lush pastures and moorlands, its mountains and lakes, its cities and its populace, along with its grandeur and its squalor, as if I were seeing it projected beyond the horizon. I perceived it with newfound eyes and a refreshed mindset, understanding it in a way I never had before, certainly loving it more deeply than I ever thought possible. After years of abstaining from a certain joy, one often finds that returning to it doesn't quite match the vivid memories built up during the absence. During the years away, the absence has allowed the imagination to embellish the experience, only for the real thing to reveal itself as somewhat mundane. While enjoyable, it doesn’t reach the heightened expectations formed in the past. Many of us have come to this realization in recent months of peace, engaging in activities we longed for during the war. Although these moments have been pleasant, they often fall short of the dreams we nurtured in the trenches of France and Flanders. Even the small joys, like the relief of not having to salute or attend medical examinations, quickly lose their novelty.

However, I recently revisited a pre-war pleasure that exceeded my expectations entirely. It was every bit as delightful as I had hoped it would be. I attended a first-class cricket match at Lord's, and it was everything I remembered and more.

There are individuals who seek to "enhance cricket," which brings to mind a particular manager to whom I once submitted a play. He courteously claimed to have enjoyed reading it, only to point out various flaws in the structure. "You have two brothers here," he observed. "They shouldn’t be brothers; they should be strangers. Then one marries the heroine, which is incorrect; it should be the other brother who does. Aunt Jane seems rather dull—what if she were arrested for bigamy? And I’d cut out your third act entirely, moving the fourth act to Monte Carlo, with the heroine facing blackmail from—what’s his name? Understand?" I acknowledged that I understood. "Are you okay with my critiques?" he asked casually. I replied that he wasn’t critiquing my work; he was crafting an entirely different story—one that I had no desire to create.

As we exited the city, I simultaneously heard three distinct sounds that together formed the essence of France. These sounds create what a poet once described as a “tangled trinity,” a concept I have no intention of unraveling. What those three elements signify, how they coexist, and whether they can somehow be harmonized is a mystery that eludes me. At that moment, I heard the brass band in the casino gardens behind me, playing a lively tune from a Parisian operetta, its spirited notes contrasted sharply with the bugles echoing from the hills above, heralding the eternal loyalty and readiness of the French people. Interwoven with these robust sounds was the faint, melodic toll of the Angelus, creating a rich tapestry of sound that enveloped me.

This convergence of symbols instilled within me a distinct sensation that I had left not only France but perhaps even the civilized world itself. The landscape around me was wild enough to support such a notion. While I have encountered taller mountains, I had never seen rocks towering so dramatically. The sheer height was astonishing, with craggy formations jutting upward like gothic church spires, and cliffs dropping abruptly and straight down, reminiscent of the fall of Satan from heaven. The experience of riding through this rugged terrain was not only awe-inspiring but also somewhat disorienting, a sensation that many who have traversed mountain roads at speed might recognize. It was as if the entire earth was revolving around my head; the hills did not merely rise and fall like massive waves but appeared to spin around me like the enormous sails of a windmill, forming a colossal wheel of angelic wings.

As we ascended further into the deepening hues of sunset, this dizzying effect intensified, blurring the boundaries between the earth and sky. Towering walls of wooded rock loomed above me, giving the impression of a great, protective canopy. I gazed at the slopes below, which seemed to cascade toward the river, only to feel as though they were climbing upward to meet the heavens. The twilight deepened, drawing the shadows longer and accentuating the stark chasms and towering spires of that surreal landscape. Above me, the imposing figure of the driver loomed, his broad back shrouded in mystery, reminiscent of the enigmatic presence of Death in Watts' painting. Feeling increasingly fanciful, I sought to ground myself in ordinary conversation. I called out to the driver in French, inquiring, "Where are you taking me?" His answer came without him turning around, delivered in the same language: "To the end of the world."

I refrained from responding, allowing him to guide the carriage up treacherous, steep paths until we stumbled upon a few lights beneath a low canopy of diminutive trees, where two children—one notably beautiful—were engaged in a game of ball. Soon, we emerged onto the main street of a quaint hamlet, where the words LE BOUT DU MONDE—French for "the end of the world"—were boldly inscribed on the wall of a local inn.

Without exchanging a word, the driver and I settled outside that inn, an unspoken understanding hanging in the air like a shared secret, natural in this ultimate location. I ordered bread and a robust red wine that bore no label, savoring its quality. Across the way stood a modest church, adorned with a cross and a rooster perched atop it. To me, this represented a fitting conclusion to the world; if the tale of existence were to end here, it would do so on a note of beauty. I mused over whether I could truly find contentment in this place, where the best elements of Christendom converged—a church, children at play, fertile land, and a tavern where men could engage in conversation. However, amid these thoughts, an unusual doubt and desire began to swell within me, prompting me to rise abruptly.

“Are you not satisfied?” my companion asked. “No,” I replied, “I am not satisfied, even at the end of the world.”

After a brief silence, I continued, “You see, there are two ends of the world. This is the wrong end of the world; at least, it is the wrong one for me. This is the French end of the world. I crave the other end of the world. Please, take me to the other end of the world.”

“The other end of the world?” he queried. “Where might that be?”

“It is in Walham Green,” I whispered, my voice hoarse with urgency. “You can see it on London’s omnibuses. ‘World’s End and Walham Green.’ While I cherish this place and its vineyards, and I admire your free peasantry, I long for the English end of the world. I appreciate you as a brother, but I yearn to encounter an English cab driver, who will humorously inquire about my fare. Your bugle calls stir my emotions, yet I find myself longing to see a London policeman. Please, oh please, take me to see a London policeman.”

The driver stood silently, his silhouette dark against the backdrop of the setting sun, and I was unable to discern whether he comprehended my sentiments. I climbed back into the carriage, hoping for understanding.

"You will grasp my feelings," I said, “if you ever find yourself an exile, even for the sake of pleasure. The yearning of a child for its mother, the longing of a man for his homeland, as a fellow countryman of yours once expressed. However, as it seems a rather lengthy journey to the English end of the world, we might as well return to Besançon."

As the stars began to twinkle among those timeless hills, I mourned for Walham Green, feeling the weight of my longing for home.

It is quite astonishing to me that there are individuals who genuinely believe that fairy tales are detrimental to children. I do not include in this group a certain man in a green tie, as I cannot truly regard him as human. However, I recently received a heartfelt letter from a woman arguing that fairy tales should not be shared with children, even if they are based on truths. Her assertion is that it is unkind to expose children to such stories because they can be frightening. One might as well argue that it is cruel to provide girls with sentimental novels since these often invoke tears. This line of reasoning stems from a profound misunderstanding of a child's nature, which has fueled numerous misguided educational theories. If we were to eliminate bogeys and goblins from children's experiences, they would simply conjure them from their imaginations. A young child, alone in the dark, can create more terrifying scenarios than the most imaginative adult. A single child can envision monsters so vast and dark that they cannot fit into any illustration and assign them names that no sane person would think to utter. Children, by their very nature, are drawn to horror; they may indulge in it even when they find it unsettling. Identifying the exact moment when true fear begins for them is as challenging as it is for us when we voluntarily step into the emotional agony of a powerful tragedy. The source of fear does not lie within fairy tales; rather, it emerges from the vastness of the human soul.

The apprehension felt by children or primitive peoples is entirely justified; they are understandably alarmed by the world around them, which can be a very intimidating place. Their discomfort with solitude is rooted in the genuine terror of being alone. Just as those without faith fear the unknown, so do the untamed souls who recognize its reality. Thus, fairy tales do not instigate fear in children nor do they introduce them to the concepts of evil or ugliness; these notions already exist within them, as they exist in the world at large. Fairy tales do not provide children with their first encounter with bogeymen. Instead, what these stories offer is a clear understanding of the possibility of vanquishing such fears. From the moment a child begins to imagine, they are already acquainted with dragons. Fairy tales introduce them to a St. George, who can slay the dragon.

“There may be Heaven; there must be Hell.”

The pessimistic view of existence has been a longstanding tradition, and new forms of spiritual exploration tend to begin with a sense of gloom. Not too long ago, people believed in no spirits. Now, there is a slow resurgence in the belief in spirits, albeit at a cautious pace.

Some have criticized spiritualism, table-tapping, and similar practices as lacking dignity, claiming that the spirits involved engage in trivialities, such as cracking jokes or dancing with furniture. I do not share this viewpoint at all. I would prefer that these spirits exhibit even more humor than they do. It is my belief that they should embrace levity and produce better jokes. Much of contemporary spiritualism, particularly its newer expressions, tends to be somber and heavy. Some ancient deities were known for their wildness, and some saints came across as overly serious; yet the spirits of today often embody a disturbing combination of both lawlessness and solemnity. Indeed, the spirits commonly encountered today are not merely devils; they are also blue devils. This encapsulates the true essence of Christmas; as long as the mythology endures, it serves as a form of joyful mythology. Personally, I maintain my belief in Santa Claus, but I am willing to extend forgiveness to those who do not share this belief during this season of grace.

For anyone who fails to grasp the shortcomings of our world, which I am striving to address, I would recommend reading Henry James's tale, “The Turn of the Screw.” It stands as one of the most impactful works ever penned, though I often question whether it should have ever been published. The narrative depicts two innocent children gradually becoming both all-knowing and foolish under the influence of the vile spirits of a groom and a governess. My reservations about whether James should have made this work public are profound (and no, it is not indecent; it pertains to spiritual matters), yet my uncertainty is so significant that I am willing to give this truly great author the benefit of the doubt. I would wholeheartedly support this work and admire it if he could write another equally compelling story featuring children and Santa Claus. If he finds this impossible, then it becomes evident that we have the capacity to tackle dark mysteries, but we struggle with those filled with joy. In this way, we are not rationalists; rather, we are diabolists.

As I pondered these thoughts while gazing into a large, fiery red blaze that stood before me like a great red angel, I realized that you may not be familiar with the concept of a red angel. However, I am certain you have encountered a blue devil—this is precisely the distinction I seek to articulate.

Recently, I found myself in conversation with a man who approached life with a measured perspective regarding a topic that had become a matter of public speculation. He remarked, "If you had asked me about the veracity of such claims four months ago, I would have responded with a definitive 'Yes.' However, after the extensive disinformation surrounding the so-called Russian army, I now require solid proof before believing anything. I was once convinced by the tales of a phantom army emerging from Archangel! There are those who assert they never bought into that narrative; some even claim they have always been skeptical. But I can assert with confidence that I was indeed a believer, and I had never encountered a rumor that seemed so well-supported by diverse and compelling evidence. Yet, it turned out to be false. Now, I find myself transformed. I no longer consider myself a believer; I have become a skeptic."

This shift in perspective is likely a common experience. A person who maintains the same level of belief today as they did six months prior is someone who has not absorbed the valuable lessons that reality imparts. We exist in an environment saturated with immense whispers, and the majority of these whispers are misleading. Even the term "Official" no longer holds the weight it used to; it is not the information I receive that I find compelling, but rather the silence surrounding what I am not told that drives my quest for truth.

Recall the infamous exchange during a libel case involving a London newspaper many years ago. When asked, "What did you instruct him to do?" the response was, "I told him to tell the truth." "The whole truth?" came the follow-up. "No, just selected truths."

In navigating the realm of rumors, we must be vigilant against our innate propensity to believe what we wish to be true. A prime example is the reported victory in Poland in November 1914. Strong evidence suggests that a significant portion of Hindenburg's forces nearly fell into a trap; had Rennenkampf arrived on schedule, the encirclement would have succeeded. However, it did not happen. Despite this, nearly every correspondent in Petrograd heralded news of a decisive victory with unwavering confidence. The correspondent for the Morning Post described it as an event "terrible yet sublime," comparing it to the devastation left by Napoleon in Russia. Even Lord Kitchener, speaking in the House of Lords, proclaimed that Russia had achieved the greatest feat of the war. Shortly thereafter, the equally unfounded rumor of Hindenburg's "victory" ignited jubilant celebrations in Berlin. This blind belief was fueled by a desire to embrace comforting narratives.

Given the financial constraints typical of a village schoolmaster, I can envision the sacrifices they made to ensure their son had a promising start. So, how do these rumors spread? There are numerous avenues. Let me illustrate one such pathway. Recently, in his critique of the war, Mr. Belloc observed the following:

"The official German communiqué released last Saturday serves as a fine example for analysis. I cite it as it was presented in the Westminster Gazette, a publication renowned for its extensive German insights since the war began."

He then proceeded to quote the communiqué. I couldn't help but smile at the cleverness of Mr. Belloc. He refers to a document that appeared in every newspaper across the nation but specifies the Westminster Gazette. The reason for this selective mention is clear: to lend credence to his parenthetical assertion about the publication's remarkable reputation for German information.

While the Westminster Gazette enjoys a solid reputation, the insinuation that it possesses some unique insight into German affairs is unfounded. Imagine if you, an ordinary citizen, were accused of having special connections with Germany during this tumultuous time. Even if you were as innocent as the Suffolk schoolmaster, you might still find yourself under the scrutiny of your fellow citizens and the watchful eyes of law enforcement.

Allow me to provide another example. A friend of mine, a journalist with liberal leanings, recently attended a private dinner with M. Painlevé, a French academician, Senator Lafontaine from Brussels, and two other deputies from France and Belgium. The following day, the Daily Express reported that he had dined with "three or four foreigners" to discuss peace. The next issue of the London Mail raised the question, "Who were the foreigners with whom he dined?" This illustrates how insinuations can breed suspicion and elevate a simple dinner into a web of speculation. My friend chose not to respond, recognizing that certain publications can be safely ignored, regardless of their claims. I mention this to demonstrate how rumors take root and evolve.

What is the lesson to be drawn from all of this? It aligns with the sentiments expressed by my earlier acquaintance. We should approach all rumors with skepticism, whether they pertain to events or individuals. When Napoleon's marshals boasted of victories, he demanded, "Show me your prisoners." Similarly, when confronted with a rumor, we should not accept it blindly. Instead, we ought to inquire, "Show me the facts." And before we embrace those facts, let us ensure they are comprehensive and not merely fragments of a larger story.

In my youth, I would share with curious owners my favorite foods—porridge, if I recall correctly—my admired heroes from both reality and fiction, my preferred virtues in women, and various other trivialities. At that age, these preferences seemed inconsequential, as I was destined to outgrow them. However, for the journalist of that era, a commitment to such definitive opinions could be perilous! If a writer were to declare in print, as I am about to do, that the daffodil is his flower of choice, merely because he spotted a lovely bowl of them on his desk while seeking inspiration, it would be unfortunate for him if a confession-album owner later revealed that he had previously sworn allegiance to the violet. Such a predicament could stifle imaginative expression. Luckily for me, I face no such constraints, and I can boldly state that the daffodil is, and has always been, my favorite flower. While many might argue in favor of the rose, I contend that the joy the daffodil brings is unparalleled, much like the pleasure a thousand pounds might provide to Rockefeller compared to the delight it offers to you or me. The daffodil arrives not only before the swallow, which is of little consequence since no one holds the swallow in disdain for that, but it also precedes the myriad flowers of summer, emerging right after a barren winter. In this way, it surpasses the rose, akin to the way an oasis in the Sahara eclipses champagne at a wedding.

Indeed, a favorite flower must undoubtedly be one that blooms in spring. This leaves us with a selection of the daffodil, violet, primrose, and crocus. The bluebell appears too late, and the cowslip is merely a lackluster version of the primrose; camellias, anemones, and other blooms belong to a separate category altogether. So, will you opt for the violet or the crocus? Or perhaps you are inclined to follow the legendary Disraeli and prefer primroses for your statue?

I write this as someone who spends the majority of his life in London, and for me, the violet, primrose, and crocus are all deficient in a vital quality—they don't display well. My choice of a favorite flower must include the ability to enhance my home; it needs to showcase its beauty effectively indoors, which necessitates a long stalk. Of all flowers, crocuses are least suited for picking. I acknowledge their charm as the first indication of spring that graces our parks, but I desire them to be closer than that. It is impossible to pluck a crocus and place it in water; it would be cruel to remove the primrose and violet from their natural habitat. In contrast, the daffodil eagerly invites being picked. That is precisely what it awaits.

"Long stalks, please." Who among us, when tasked by a loved one to gather flowers for the home, has not been given such a directive? And is there any stalk that can rival the daffodil’s in terms of length, sturdiness, and beauty? Other flowers require foliage to enhance their appearance, but daffodils can stand alone in a vase, their green and yellow attire bringing the essence of spring into any room. A house adorned with daffodils feels alive, regardless of whether the sun shines outside. Daffodils in a green bowl—let the snow fall, if it must.

Wordsworth composed a poem dedicated to daffodils. In fact, he wrote verses about most flowers. To be unique, a plant must surely be one that has never inspired his pen. However, he did not write about daffodils in a bowl. The daffodils I cherish are stationary, while those celebrated by Wordsworth danced along the banks of Ullswater, swaying and fluttering in the breeze. He suggests that even he might have felt jovial in their presence—a daunting thought, which makes me relieved to have my daffodils safely indoors. When he first encountered them, he gazed with wonder, unaware of the wealth that such a sight would bestow upon him. Technically, he hadn’t gained anything in that moment, but he must have recognized from past experiences with daisies and celandines that it was good for a certain amount of inspiration.

To him, a simple daffodil constituted enough material for a slender volume priced at two shillings and fourpence.

You might argue that I am in no better position, but unlike him, I have never criticized others for merely perceiving a primrose as just a primrose.

Regardless of whether you prefer them as I do—indoors—or as Wordsworth did—outdoors—the name of the flower merits attention. Is there a more beautiful name in existence than daffodil? Say it aloud, then compare it to "agapanthus" or "chrysanthemum" or any other name you choose, and see if the daffodil does not come out on top.

Pansies, lilies, kingcups, daisies,  
Let them bask in their praise;  
As long as the sun sets,  
Primroses will enjoy their glory;  
While violets retain their place in history;  
But for filling my bowls with flowers,  
I only want the daffodil.

As Wordsworth should have articulated.
