Recently, I found myself in a rather precarious situation involving two enthusiastic police officers while wandering in a Yorkshire wood. During my holiday, I had indulged in a medley of enjoyable activities, duties, and explorations—what one might refer to in a more mundane sense as doing nothing. At that moment, I was attempting to throw a large Swedish knife at a tree, practicing what I had hoped would be a useful skill in knife-throwing, reminiscent of the violent escapades found in Stevenson’s novels.

Out of the blue, I was approached by two policemen who seemed to emerge from the very fabric of the forest itself. Their presence, in some inexplicable way, sparked memories of joyful Elizabethan comedies. They bombarded me with questions about the knife, my identity, the reason behind my actions, my address, profession, religious beliefs, opinions regarding the Japanese war, and even the name of my favorite cat. They also accused me of damaging the tree, a claim I regrettably had to refute since I had failed to hit it. Nonetheless, the philosophical implications of this encounter were intriguing. After a lively conversation lasting about thirty minutes, during which I showcased an envelope and an unfinished poem—read with great scrutiny, I hope to some benefit—the elder of the two officers ultimately became convinced of my authenticity. He accepted that I was indeed a journalist for the DAILY NEWS, a revelation that seemed to instill a common fear among those in authority, and acknowledged my residence with certain well-known and affluent individuals in the area.

The leading officer grew increasingly amiable, even claiming to be a reader of my work. Once that admission was made, everything appeared to be resolved. They decided to let me go without further ado.

“But,” I inquired, “what about the tree that has suffered at my hand? You rushed in like gallant knights to save that Dryad, tethered to the ground. You, the noble protectors of humanity, are not deceived by the apparent stillness of nature, a stillness akin to the silence of a waterfall—a profound and unyielding quietude. You understand that a tree is merely a creature anchored to the earth by one leg. You would not permit marauders armed with Swedish knives to spill the verdant lifeblood of such a being. Yet, if that is the case, why am I not in custody? Where are my shackles? Surely, the facts I have provided you—that my name is Chesterton, that I am a journalist residing with the esteemed Mr. Blank of Ilkley—should not alter your assessment of whether I have committed an act of cruelty against this vegetable life. The tree remains damaged, regardless of its proud reflection that it was harmed by a gentleman associated with the Liberal press. The bark will not heal faster simply because the injury was inflicted by someone staying with Mr. Blank in Ilkley. The tragedy of that tree, now a mere shadow of its former grandeur, laid low by my clumsy throw, cannot simply be overlooked due to my temporary association with affluent people. It is astonishing that you lack the authority to detain even the most prominent and fashionable individuals for such a transgression. If that is the case, what prompted your intervention in my actions?”

I directed the latter part of my speech to the silent woods, as the two policemen had disappeared almost as swiftly as they had arrived. It’s entirely possible that they were fairies. If that were the case, their rather illogical understanding of crime, law, and accountability would receive a whimsical explanation; perhaps if I had lingered until moonrise, I might have witnessed small police officers frolicking on the grass, or scuttling about with glow-worm belts, arresting grasshoppers for damaging blades of grass. However, assuming they were indeed genuine policemen, I found myself in a peculiar predicament. I had been accused of something that was either an offense or was not. I was released because I managed to demonstrate my connection to a prominent household. The implication was unsettlingly clear: either throwing a knife in a secluded wood is not inherently wrong, or knowing a wealthy individual somehow exonerates one from guilt. Imagine, for instance, a much poorer individual—a laborer tirelessly seeking work, frequently changing accommodations, possibly even struggling to pay rent. If this person had been overcome with the vibrant allure of the ancient wood and engaged in the same knife-throwing, yet could only describe his last dwelling as a miserable place from which he had been evicted. As I strolled home through a dimming and purplish twilight, I pondered how he would have fared in a similar situation.

Moral reflections abound in this scenario. We English often take pride in our supposed illogicality; while this may not be inherently harmful, it can lead to greater issues. There is no deep spiritual malaise in boasting about one’s flaws, but when individuals begin to brag about their virtues, they become intolerable. However, I must assert that illogicality within our laws or our constitution could pose serious dangers, especially if a significant national vice or collective temptation arises that many exploit amid the disarray. Much like a drunk person requires stringent guidelines, a sober individual may follow their instincts with more freedom.

Consider one of the absurdities in British law—take, for example, the stipulation that a person ceasing to be a Member of Parliament must become the Steward of the Chiltern Hundreds, a title initially intended to curb some banditry in that region. Clearly, such illogicalities carry little weight since there is no substantial incentive to abuse them. Former MPs have no overwhelming desire to hunt down robbers in the hills. However, should there arise a genuine danger that respectable, elderly politicians leaving public office might want to exploit this loophole (perhaps if it were financially beneficial), then dismissing the illogicality as inconsequential would be naive. In such a case, the illogical nature of the law would matter significantly, as it could become a justification for misconduct. Only the most virtuous among us can lead wild lives without consequence.

This dynamic is precisely what occurs in situations involving police inquiries, such as the one I’ve recounted. A deeper national flaw emerges—far greater than the vice of alcohol—namely, the tendency to hold gentlemen in high regard. Snobbishness, much like intoxication, possesses a certain grand allure. Yet it harbors a uniquely insidious quality that often seeps through the actions of even the kindest individuals, those with open hearts and welcoming homes. This pervasive English vice deserves scrutiny, more so than any contagious disease. If one were to distill the essence of the worst and most corrupt elements of England into simple terms, it would not be found in foul language or vulgar disputes. Instead, it resides in the fact that when the best kind of working-class individual seeks to commend someone, they refer to them as “a gentleman.” It never occurs to them to equate that praise with titles such as “marquis” or “privy councillor”—they are merely designating a social rank, not genuinely evaluating a person’s character. This enduring temptation to idolize social status inevitably influences and distorts our policing methods.

In conclusion, we must be vigilant and precise in our reasoning, for we must self-monitor our inclinations. The power of wealth, especially in its most nefarious forms, is on the rise in our contemporary world. A truly good and just society, devoid of such temptations, might not require strict regulations to safeguard against the influence of powerful financiers. However, the absence of this corruption would likely have led to a more decisive response long before.

Two soldiers, clearly siblings, were positioned at the entrance of a railway carriage—one seated within the compartment, the other standing on the platform.

"Promise me you won't forget to write, Bill," the one on the platform urged.

"I won’t," replied Bill. "I’ll be back at—tonight, and I’ll make sure to write everyone tomorrow. But, goodness, what a task! There's Mother, the missus, Bob and Sarah, Aunt Jane, Uncle Jim, and—well, you know the whole crowd. You’ve had to do it, Sam."

"Indeed," Sam said with a hint of regret; “it’s quite a puzzle.”

"And if you write to one and overlook another, they all get upset," Bill continued. "But I make sure to mention everyone. I’ll write 'love to Sarah' and 'hope Aunt Jane’s cold is better,' and that sort of thing—it helps fill the page. But I’m stumped if I can think of anything else. I just start with 'I hope this finds you well, as it leaves me at present,' and then I’m out of steam. What else can I say?"

"Nothing," Sam said with a sigh. "I just sit there staring at the paper, but nothing comes to me. It feels like my mind is as empty as a drum."

"Same here. It’s not like writing love letters. Back when I was doing that, it was easy. If I hit a wall, I’d just fill half a page with doodles, and it looked just fine. But writing to Mother, the missus, Sarah, Jim, and the others is a whole different ballgame. You can’t just fill it with doodles; that would look ridiculous."

"Quite right," Sam agreed.

As the train began to pull away, the soldier inside settled back into his seat, pulled out a cigarette, and lit it. I learned that he had been at the front twice and was now on sick leave. He had participated in the battle of Mons, experienced the retreat to the Marne, advanced to the Aisne, fought in the first battle of Ypres, and engaged in the fighting at Festubert. He had been present for some of the defining events of history, yet when it came to writing a letter, even to his wife, he found himself at a loss for words. He was much like a woman mentioned by Horace Walpole, whose correspondence began and ended with the statement: "I write to you because I have nothing to do: I finish because I have nothing to say."

It seems that never before has there been such a surge in letter-writing as there is today, and much of it is well-crafted, as evidenced in newspapers. However, the experience of my companion on the train reflects the struggles of countless young men who, for the first time, are eager to express themselves in writing but find that they lack the ability to convey their thoughts. This is not due to a lack of intelligence; rather, the act of putting pen to paper leaves them paralyzed. They struggle to translate the vibrant atmosphere surrounding them into concrete words. They require encouragement to articulate their feelings. Once prompted, they can articulate their thoughts perfectly well, but without that nudge, they remain silent.

In a broader context, it can be argued that letter-writing is a dying art. The introduction of the penny post and the fast pace of modern life have contributed to its decline. When renowned writers such as Madame de Sévigny, Cowper, Horace Walpole, Byron, Lamb, and the Carlyles penned their memorable letters, society was much more leisurely, allowing for the indulgence of writing to friends. The expense of mailing a letter made it a significant endeavor. If you could only send a letter once a month or even every six months, and at a high cost, it became a matter of great importance. The less fortunate, of course, could hardly partake in the luxury of letter-writing. De Quincey recounts how a century ago, the rural families of Lakeland would avoid postal fees. A letter arriving by stagecoach would be received by a mother who, upon glancing at the address and recognizing a certain mark indicating her son was well, would return it unopened to the carrier. In those days, receiving a letter was an event.

Today, however, with the ability to send a letter across the globe for a mere penny and postal services delivering multiple times a day, many of us do not take letter-writing seriously. Carlyle foresaw that the introduction of the penny post would diminish the art of letter-writing by making it too affordable. "I shall send a penny letter next time," he wrote to his mother as cheap postage was on the horizon, predicting that people would no longer feel compelled to write meaningful letters when they could send them for next to nothing. He was correct; the telegraph, the telephone, and the postcard have further contributed to the decline of this once revered form of communication. The rarity or difficulty of obtaining something often elevates its value. If diamonds were as common as pebbles, we wouldn’t bother to pick them up.

Yet, the situation for Bill, Sam, and countless others today diverges from this trend. They aren’t aiming to craft literary masterpieces; rather, they wish to share their experiences with loved ones back home, to convey something about their lives and the monumental events they are part of. However, the enormity of those experiences often eludes their expression. They should not feel pressured to articulate the grand narratives; instead, the essence of letter-writing resides in the small, intimate details. Bill might not be able to narrate the retreat from Mons, but he could share, as he did with me, the story of the blister on his heel, his yearning for a cigarette, the endless marches that left him exhausted, losing his friend at Le Cateau, or how his boot sole fell off at Meaux. Through such mundane details, he would paint a vivid picture of the great retreat.

To craft an effective letter, one must approach the task with a light and casual attitude. It is essential to be personal rather than abstract. One should not dismiss the significance of everyday occurrences as too trivial to mention. Instead, one should recognize that these small moments are precisely what we discuss at home. By sharing these, the recipient gains a sense of presence; they can envision the writer, hear their voice, and understand their circumstances. This is the true purpose of a letter. Keats encapsulated this concept beautifully in one of his extensive letters addressed to his brother George and his wife in America, where he expressed the depth of familial affection that characterized his nature. He described a visit to his mother, the laughter over his poor jokes, their outing for tea at Mrs. Millar’s, and how the interplay of light and shadow struck them as they passed through the Horse Guards. He continued, "I intend to write you such volumes that it will be impossible for me to keep any order or method in what I write; that will come first which is uppermost in my mind, not that which is uppermost in my heart—besides I should wish to give you a picture of our lives here whenever by a touch I can do it; even as you must see by the last sentence our walk past Whitehall all in good health and spirits—this I am certain of because I felt so much pleasure from the simple idea of your playing a game of cricket."

This illustrates the recipe from one of the masters of the craft. A letter written in such a manner bridges the gap of distance; it sustains the personal exchanges and intimate connections that separation interrupts, ensuring one’s presence is felt even in their absence. It should never be too simple, too ordinary, or too conversational. Its familiarity is not a weakness but rather its greatest strength. Should it strive for order, grandeur, or elaboration, it may turn into a fine essay yet will undoubtedly fail as a letter.

The Bar has always struck me as the most esteemed of professions, a field where its practitioners can maintain their dignity, no matter the circumstances. This is not the case with other professions. A teacher can be derisively referred to as an usher, a doctor may be humorously branded a licensed killer, and solicitors often face criminal charges for mishandling trust funds, earning the moniker of mere attorneys. Civil servants, on the other hand, are often seen as lethargic, waking only for their pensions at retirement. However, barristers stand apart from this mockery; the only jest one might make about them is to refer to them as “my learned friend.” Their claim to professionalism carries more weight than that of an actor. The reason behind this perception eludes me—perhaps it is simply because they don their top hats while walking through the Temple.

Many of my acquaintances have dabbled in the legal profession, having “eaten dinners” at the Inns of Court, making it challenging to voice any criticism of their chosen path. Additionally, one can never be too certain when one might find themselves in need of legal representation. Nonetheless, I will take the plunge and put the barrister on trial. "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, consider this well-tailored individual before you. What can we say about him?"

To begin, let us reflect on our expectations from a profession. First and foremost, we undoubtedly seek a livelihood, yet I believe we desire something beyond mere financial compensation. If offered a thousand pounds a year to walk daily from Charing Cross to Barnet, although poverty might compel acceptance, we would not take pride in such a vocation. We would rather earn that same sum by engaging in work that contributes positively to society. A person of any sensitivity would only find a walking profession bearable if they could convince themselves that their efforts revived the forgotten art of walking or highlighted the overlooked attractions of Barnet. Ideally, after numerous journeys, curious individuals might begin to follow, intrigued by the purpose behind those walks, discovering the old Norman church at the crossroads or, at the very least, developing a healthier appetite for their dinners. In essence, one must believe they are acting not solely for personal gain but for the benefit of the community as well.

A physician may charge fees, yet their motivation lies in alleviating suffering. A teacher earns a living through instruction, but they see themselves as champions of education. Artists, regardless of their chosen medium, seek to convey a message to the world, sharing their truths—which may benefit them but are not solely for their profit. All these professions, along with countless others, possess an inherent nobility. We embark on these paths filled with aspirations, promising ourselves that we will remain true to our ideals and not compromise our principles for personal interests. Yet, we inevitably stumble. The painter, lured by financial success, churns out repetitive works. The physician prioritizes bedside manner over groundbreaking research. The teacher abandons innovative educational theories to conform to administrative standards. Our failures do not stem from the ignobility of our professions; rather, they arise from our inability to stay true to our aspirations. The guiding light remains for those who seek it; it continues to beckon.

Now, what about the Bar? Does a barrister strive for anything beyond personal advancement? What ideals do they pursue? It matters little whether they succeed more or less frequently than others in reaching these ideals; what I seek to understand is what motivates them. In those quiet moments when we are alone, stripped of external validation, we sometimes confront the unsettling thought of our contributions. If a barrister experiences such an introspective moment, what reassurance can they draw from it? The only solace may lie in the belief that they are contributing to the administration of Justice. To take pride in their profession, to feel justified in their choices during those solitary reflections, they must convince themselves that they play a vital role in upholding legal rights and addressing legal wrongs.

However, this is not enough. Just as a doctor, through knowledge and experience, becomes more effective in combating illness—benefiting both themselves and the field of medicine—so must the barrister be able to assert that their growing skill as an advocate enhances their capacity to serve the ideal of Justice. But can they genuinely make that claim? I struggle to see how they could. While their increasing expertise may serve their interests and those of their clients, it does not necessarily advance the ideal of Justice itself. Consider a hypothetical case, Smith v. Jones. Counsel represents Smith. After reviewing the facts, he concludes, “Legally speaking, the odds are against us. However, sentiment might sway the jury in our favor. It’s worth a shot.” He proceeds, and if he is sufficiently skilled, he secures a victory. A personal success for him, but what becomes of the ideal? Did he ever contemplate, “I must do my utmost for my client, even if he is in the wrong, and hope for a loss?” I suspect not. The prevailing ethos of the Bar teaches that the focus should be on winning, not on pursuing justice. Ultimately, what is the true pursuit of a barrister? What does the Bar provide beyond the allure of financial rewards?

Earlier, I inquired about the ideals of a barrister. Let’s reframe the question: What does it mean to be an ideal barrister? If we were to casually define an ideal doctor, we wouldn’t necessarily envision a prestigious figure on Harley Street. An ideal teacher does not equate to the Headmaster of Eton or the proprietor of a lucrative preparatory school. Yet, can we conceive of an ideal barrister that is not synonymous with success in terms of wealth and status? The enthusiastic novice writer might aspire to emulate Francis Thompson over Sir Hall Caine, and an aspiring clergyman might find inspiration in the life of Father Damien rather than the Archbishop of Canterbury. But what aspiration can a budding barrister realistically pursue, save for the star of financial success? If they do not envision themselves as Sir Edward Carson, it’s likely because they believe that the more effective path lies in mirroring Sir John Simon’s approach.

There may be alternative responses to the queries I have posed, yet questioning the necessity of barristers in the administration of law does not provide an answer. I cannot fathom how such a system could function without them, just as I find it hard to imagine how roads could be kept clean without someone to do the work. However, this does not prevent me from expressing my belief that road-sweeping is an unappealing profession. Similarly, I feel entitled to share my perspective regarding the Bar. In my view, it offers only tangible victories and lacks spiritual fulfillment. There exists no standard by which its members can be measured except for earthly success, and there is no space within its ranks for altruism or idealism. For these reasons, I assert that the Bar does not belong among the noble professions.

What is it that we all seek? I suspect that the answer is surprisingly close. As a child, I imagined that Heaven or Fairyland—whatever I chose to call it—lay just behind me, which is why I could never quite glimpse it, no matter how many times I twisted and turned in an attempt to catch it off guard. I envisioned a person perpetually spinning around on one foot, like a top, in an effort to discover that hidden world that perpetually eluded him. Perhaps this is the reason the world spins. It is as if the world is forever attempting to glance over its shoulder in pursuit of the elusive realm that it cannot exist without.

In any event, as I mentioned earlier, I believe we must always envision the ultimate aim of our endeavors as something curiously close at hand. While science takes pride in discussing the vast distances of its celestial bodies and the daunting remoteness of the phenomena it examines, poetry and religion insist on the immediacy of their subjects, often highlighting their unnerving nearness. The Kingdom of Heaven is always described as being "At Hand," while Looking-glass Land is merely a reflection through the glass. Thus, it wouldn’t astonish me if the next turn down a street led me to the very center of that labyrinth where all the mystics seem to be lost. I wouldn’t even be surprised if, upon rounding a corner in Fleet Street, I stumbled upon an even stranger lamp; nor would I be shocked if I found myself in Elfland after the next turn.

However, what did catch me off guard recently was something far more unexpected. I ventured out of Fleet Street and unexpectedly found myself in England.

The peculiar shock I felt likely merits some explanation. Even in the bleakest or most disappointing moments of English life, there is one fundamental truth about our nation that must not be overlooked: England is not nearly as foolish as it appears. The various representations of England, the external symbols of the country, often mislead the observer. England operates as an oligarchy, deliberately presenting an elite that seems inferior to the general populace.

Consider the discourse in the House of Commons; it is not only poorer than the speaking found in many smaller debate clubs or informal dinners, but it also falls short of what is deemed acceptable in almost every other venue. It seems that my countrymen prefer this solemn absurdity at the higher echelons of our national life. It may be a curious sight to witness the blind leading the blind, but England offers a stranger spectacle: the blind attempting to guide those who can see. This, in fact, is an understatement. The ignorance displayed by political leaders is often a manufactured and deliberate facade. If one is fortunate enough to engage in genuine conversation with a politician, they may find themselves astonished by the intelligent insights that emerge. Initially, it can be unsettling. I have never been close enough to one of these individuals to question why they choose to feign ignorance while in Parliament.

The same holds true for the electorate. The average voter seems to cast their ballot beneath their own potential; they engage in the act of voting with only a fraction of their mind. Voting should encompass the entirety of an individual—just as one should worship or marry with their whole being. When casting a vote, one ought to engage their intellect and emotions, their spirit and physical instincts, their appreciation for beauty and their love for music. If they have ever witnessed a breathtaking sunset, the vibrant hues should influence their choice at the polls. If they have been moved by beautiful melodies, those songs should echo in their ears as they make that sacred mark. Yet, the challenge confronting English democracy at every election is that it often represents something less than its true potential. The issue is not merely that a minority of the electorate participates; rather, it is that a minority of those who vote truly engage with the process.

This is the tragedy of England: one cannot accurately judge the nation based on its most visible leaders. The stereotypes we encounter do not encapsulate the reality. On the occasion I reference, I discovered this to be particularly true of a once-vibrant middle class, which I assumed had nearly disappeared from existence. It appeared to me that the primary representatives of this class had all drifted in different directions; they had either pursued the allure of the Smart Set or sought the simplicity of the Simple Life. Personally, I find it difficult to favor one over the other; those individuals may keep either—or, more likely, both—alternatively succumbing to the sickness of each. Yet, all the notable figures who seem to embody the middle class have either adopted the monocle of Mr. Chamberlain or the singular vision of Mr. Bernard Shaw.

This old class I speak of lacks a true representative. Its sustenance was ample but unpretentious; its meals were simple yet devoid of trends. It took politics seriously, and when it engaged in public discourse, it committed the faux pas of attempting to articulate well. I believed that this earnest political England had all but vanished. Yet, as I said, I made a turn away from Fleet Street and discovered a room filled with that very essence.

At the front of the room stood a chair once occupied by Johnson. This was a club where Wilkes had addressed the masses in a time when even the most disreputable among us exuded a sense of vigor. However, one could argue that these historical references might merely denote a bygone era. The most remarkable aspect was that the hall resonated with the passion, sincerity, fervor, and oratory characteristic of the eighteenth century. The club members represented a spectrum of opinions, yet not a single speech struck me with the dissonance of unreality that often accompanies hearing skilled speakers express sentiments I share. The Toryism present in this club mirrored that of Johnson: a Toryism that embraced humor and appealed to humanity. The democracy found here resembled that of Wilkes: a democracy capable of crafting epigrams and engaging in duels, a democracy that could confront challenges head-on and withstand slander; it was the democracy of Wilkes—or, perhaps more accurately, that of Fox.

One element in particular stirred my soul, connecting me to my ancestors. Each speaker, regardless of their eloquence, rose to address the audience with raw passion, intent on dismantling their opponent—not through mockery, but via genuine eloquence. This marks a significant decline in our modern political discourse. Today, a speaker does not become more oratorical as their sincerity deepens. An eighteenth-century orator, when genuinely enraged, would search for grand words to obliterate their adversary. In contrast, the contemporary speaker resorts to petty language to undermine their opponent. The rhetoric now resides in the formalities that go unheard. When a politician—be it Mr. Chamberlain, a moderate figure, or a more radical socialist—becomes truly sincere, their discourse degenerates into something coarse, punctuated by phrases like, “Where do we come in?” or “It’s your money they want.”

The individuals in this eighteenth-century club were entirely of that bygone era; each one stood up visibly trembling with emotion, striving to vanquish their counterpart through the power of articulate expression. I found myself debating with them on the topic of Home Rule, and ultimately expressed my belief that the English aristocracy held disdain for the idea of an Irish Parliament because it would resemble their own club.

As I exited the club and stepped back into Fleet Street under the dim glow of a streetlamp, I stumbled upon a crude poster about Wastrels, claiming that London was rising against something hardly anyone had heard of. Suddenly, it struck me, almost like a vivid tableau: the modern world resembles a vast and tempestuous ocean, teeming with monstrous, living entities. And upon this turbulent sea rests a fragile, thin layer of ice, composed of deceitful wealth and duplicitous journalism.

Standing there in the shadows, I could almost hear that ice beginning to crack.

Not long ago, I shared a piece titled "The Extraordinary Cabman" in these pages. Today, I have the opportunity to recount an even more remarkable experience involving a cab. What made this cab so extraordinary was its distinct aversion to me; it ejected me forcefully right in the middle of the Strand. If my esteemed readers of the DAILY NEWS possess the romantic spirit (and wealth) that I assume they do, then I suspect this is an experience that is not entirely rare. It stands to reason that many of them may have also found themselves unceremoniously tossed from cabs across London. Yet, for the sake of those few who remain untouched by this particular luxury, I will describe the psychological journey I underwent when my hansom cab collided with a motor omnibus, leaving me to wonder about the fate of my dignity.

The innate charm of the hansom cab is something I need not elaborate on—the quintessential modern creation that, when our era is reflected upon, will be regarded alongside the grandeur of the Parthenon. It embodies modernity in its swiftness and secrecy. My particular hansom cab exemplified these traits, though it met with unfortunate circumstances as well. It is a uniquely English invention, absent in foreign lands, rooted in a beautiful and romantic country where most inhabitants pretend to possess wealth beyond their means. The hansom is both comfortable and reckless, and this juxtaposition encapsulates the very essence of England. Despite my appreciation for the many virtues of a hansom cab, I had yet to confront its full spectrum of possibilities—or, as contemporary expressions go, its various aspects. My previous assertions regarding the merits of such vehicles were made while they were upright. Therefore, allow me to convey my feelings during that fateful moment when I was unceremoniously ejected from a hansom cab for what I hope is the first and last time. While Polycrates tossed one of his rings into the sea to appease the Fates, I have metaphorically cast a hansom cab into the depths, and I trust the Fates are satisfied, even if they do not appreciate being told so.

Yesterday afternoon, I found myself riding in a hansom cab, descending one of the gentle inclines toward the Strand, engrossed in the pleasure and surprise of reading one of my own commendable articles. Suddenly, the horse faltered, stumbled briefly on the rough stones, and then regained its footing. This was a common occurrence for the horses in my cabs, and I had grown accustomed to enjoying my articles regardless of the vehicle's angle. Thus, I thought nothing of the horse's momentary struggle. However, a glance at the faces of the pedestrians revealed a stark change; they were transfixed with fear, as if struck by a bolt of lightning. One man even rushed into the street, his arm raised as if to deflect an impending blow, attempting to halt the horse's advance. It was then I understood that the reins had slipped from my grasp, and in an instant, the horse surged forward like a bolt of lightning. I strive to recount events as they appeared to me, acknowledging that I may have overlooked or misstated numerous details, and that many aspects might have been distorted in the chaos of that wild dash down the street. I once referred to a past experience as “A Fragment of Fact”; this moment, too, qualifies as a fragment of reality, though it is one that I could never have anticipated at the street's end.

I am a firm believer in addressing those who already hold certain convictions, for I have often found that they do not fully grasp the depth of their own beliefs. This has led me to assert that democracy encompasses a meaning that often eludes those who champion it. Ordinary expressions, proverbs, and common phrases frequently harbor insights that many who repeat them fail to recognize. Take, for instance, the notion that a person in imminent danger can witness their entire life flash before their eyes in an instant. In the stark, literal sense, this is an outright fabrication. No one can claim that during a crisis, they meticulously recalled every event, every ticket they ever purchased to Wimbledon, or the countless times they shared brown bread and butter.

Yet, as my cab hurtled toward the bustling traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is indeed a kernel of truth nestled within that phrase, as is often the case with popular expressions. In those fleeting, shrill moments, I experienced a rapid succession of fundamental perspectives. I went through what might be described as five distinct religions in the span of just a few seconds. Initially, I found myself engulfed in pure Paganism, better known among sincere individuals as sheer terror. This state was soon succeeded by a mindset that, while real, defies proper nomenclature. The ancients might have referred to it as Stoicism, and perhaps it aligns with what some German philosophers mean when they discuss Pessimism. It was an empty acceptance of whatever fate had in store, as if I had transcended the significance of it all. Strangely, this was followed by an intense contrary feeling—that life mattered immensely, and yet it was something beyond mere tragedy. I sensed that life was far too vital to ever be reduced to anything less than life itself. I hope this realization was a reflection of Christianity; at least, it coincided with the moment of our collision with the omnibus.

In what felt like a surreal twist, the hansom cab seemed to topple over me, enveloping me like a massive hood. I soon found myself crawling out from beneath it, in such undignified postures that I must have inadvertently contributed significantly to the cause championed by the Anti-Puritan League, with which I recently aligned myself—namely, the pursuit of the people’s pleasures. Regarding my demeanor upon emerging from beneath the cab, I must confess two things, both shared solely for the sake of psychological inquiry. First, just moments before the collision, I had been in a seemingly serene state of mind; however, upon standing up and realizing I had sustained only minor cuts, I began, much like St. Peter, to unleash a torrent of curses. A man approached, offering me a newspaper or some item I had dropped. I can vividly recall condemning that paper to a fate of irredeemable spiritual ruin. I now deeply regret this outburst, and I extend my apologies to both the man and the newspaper. The reason for this inexplicable anger escapes me, but I mention it as a psychological curiosity. This outburst was swiftly followed by a wave of hilarity; I made so many absurd jokes to the policeman that he succumbed to laughter, much to the chagrin of the little boys in the street who had previously taken him seriously.

There was another peculiar aspect of this incident that I mention as an intriguing facet of human psychology—or perhaps a deficiency thereof. Every three minutes or so, I found myself reminding the policeman that I had yet to pay the cabman and fervently hoped he would not suffer a financial loss. The officer reassured me that everything would be fine and that the cabman would show up. However, it wasn’t until half an hour later that it struck me with a jolt that the cabman might have been at risk of losing more than just a small fare; he had faced danger alongside me. In my mind, I had instinctively elevated the cabman to a status akin to that of a deity, impervious to mishaps. I promptly began to make inquiries and was relieved to learn that my concerns had been unfounded.

From that moment on, I gained a deeper and more nuanced understanding of those who meticulously adhere to the lesser details while neglecting the more significant matters at hand; I, too, felt the weight of guilt for having owed a mere half-crown to a person who might have been injured or worse. Some dedicated gentlemen in white coats at Charing Cross Hospital attended to my minor injuries, after which I stepped back out into the bustling Strand. A sense of unnatural youth enveloped me, igniting a yearning for uncharted experiences. Thus, to mark the start of a new chapter in my life, I climbed into yet another hansom cab.
